News.title: I got addicted to camping gas at 14 and had to pull out all my teeth
News.content:
I got addicted to camping gas at 14 and had to pull out all my teeth

Sarah Clarke says no one ever stopped her buying the cans despite it being illegal to sell to children

View 5 Images Sarah Clarke, 38, started using butane gas, as a recreational drug at age 14

A woman who was hooked on £1.25 camping gas, buying up to 12 cans a day, ripped all of her teeth out after the habit led to severe toothache. Sarah Clarke, 38, started using butane, used for portable cooking stoves and some cigarette lighters, as a recreational drug at age 14, and by 18 she was hooked.

‌



The homemaker, from Leicester, said that no shop owner ever questioned her about her purchases, despite it being illegal to sell the gas to anyone under 18. After inhaling the gas every day for 15 years, Sarah was able to kick her habit in 2022, as it was her mum's dying wish.

‌



She has irreversible health issues, including nerve damage and early-onset Parkinson's. Sarah is calling for tighter restrictions on the sale of butane gas. She said: "The first time I did it, I felt like it numbed everything that was going on in my life. I could go to the shops and easily buy 12 cans at age 15. No one would stop me.

‌



It's not what you eat but when you eat, keep an eye on your belly not BMI, using the internet makes you grumpy, and cutting your run short is dangerous = all this and more in our science newsletter

View 5 Images The cans are cheap and easy to buy

"I don't understand why it's still so easy and cheap to buy. I'm 38, but I look 78. The damage I've done to myself is irreversible."

‌



Sarah was first introduced to butane gas at age 14 by one of her friends, who was experimenting after finding a canister of the flammable gas in their parents' home.

Sarah continued to experiment by using the gas with friends every now and again until she was 16, and she started to lean on the drug and use it on her own. She would go to the local corner shop and buy 8 to 10 cans for £1.25 each.

View 5 Images Sarah wants to be drug-free

‌



One can would last Sarah around an hour, and she would immediately move on to the next one. She would hide the empty cans in the bottom of her wardrobe, some of which were discovered by her mum.

"She was so shocked when she found them, but she just thought I was experimenting with friends. She had no idea how bad it was", Sarah said. By the age of 18, Sarah was getting through up to 12 cans of butane gas per day, and wouldn't leave the house at all, except to go to the shops to get more of the drug.

Sarah's drug misuse has caused a variety of health problems, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a lung condition which makes it difficult to breathe, as airways are damaged. She also suffers from early-onset Parkinson's, nerve damage, and memory loss, and is constantly falling over and injuring herself, as she has a complete lack of balance.

‌



View 5 Images Sarah has been using the gas for years

"I'm on 11 different medications for a 38-year-old - that's shocking", she said "I struggle to eat proper food because I can't get it down my throat."

In 2022, Sarah suffered from a severe toothache due to the effects of her butane gas misuse. As she couldn't get an appointment at the dentist, she leaned on butane gas even more to numb the pain and eventually ended up ripping all of her own teeth out to stop the aching.

‌



View 5 Images Sarah Clarke, 38

Sarah now has no teeth at all and is waiting for a set of false teeth on the NHS. In March 2022, Sarah lost her mum, and her dying wish was for Sarah to stop using butane gas. Seeing her mum lying on her deathbed, she had an epiphany and decided to go completely cold turkey.

"I know they say that's not advisable, but it's worked so far, and it's been almost four years now", she said. Sarah's grief helped her to stay distracted from her withdrawal, as did focusing on tasks such as cleaning the house and taking her dog for a walk, but she struggled to find any support to guide her through her recovery.

Article continues below

"You just need a bit of courage, and if you want to do it, you will do it, but there is no help out there", she said. “There are no forums or anything. I’ve tried looking for a case similar to mine, but I can’t find anything.”

News.title: 'I've never smoked but now I've got incurable lung cancer'
News.content:
'I've never smoked but now I've got incurable lung cancer'

Jade Fardon had a cough she couldn't shift alongside other symptoms

View 4 Images Jade Fardon in hospital (Image: Jade Fardon/SWNS)

A woman who developed a cough was diagnosed with incurable lung cancer - despite never having smoked. Jade Fardon, 33, couldn't shift her cough, but doctors reassured her it would go away on its own.

‌



It did, but it came back again and again over the years and she returned to the GP several times to have her chest checked. She began to notice other things too - a hoarse voice, some nausea, increasing fatigue and night sweats.

‌



By April 2022 she compiled a list of all her symptoms for the GP and this time was referred for a CT scan, which showed extensive cancer across both her lungs. Jade, who was then 29, had never smoked and lived a healthy, active life.

‌



It's not what you eat but when you eat, keep an eye on your belly not BMI, using the internet makes you grumpy, and cutting your run short is dangerous = all this and more in our science newsletter

She didn't need chemotherapy, but was given a daily cancer drug to take, which shrank the tumours and prevented them from growing. Almost two years on, metastases were found in her brain during a routine MRI scan and she needed gamma knife therapy - a precise, intensive form of radiation - to attack the lesions, which initially appeared to have been successful.

But she learned one lesion had continued to progress since the treatment, when she suffered a brain bleed later that year and she needed brain surgery to remove the lesion. She has been given new long-term medication to keep her condition stable, is regularly monitored and is raising awareness of lung cancer in young people.

‌



View 4 Images Jade began to notice other things too - a hoarse voice, some nausea, increasing fatigue and night sweats (Image: Jade Fardon/SWNS)

Jade, a business change manager from Watford, Hertfordshire, said: "I had a cough, but everyone thought it was Covid and because I'm relatively young, when it went away, I didn't suspect anything. When I went to the doctor with my symptoms two years later, I did suspect it might be cancer, but not lung cancer.

"When I got the results of my CT scan, it was already stage four and it was very scary, I was shocked and in a bit of denial. As treatment started, for a long time, I didn't want to hear the word 'cancer' at all.

‌



"When I went on the first drug, it shrank the tumours. So when I found out they found metastases in my brain, I had to go through all those scary feelings again.

"But this condition has been incurable since the very start when I was diagnosed, so this is my new life. Sometimes I pause and feel sad, but anyone could think that. Now I want to challenge assumptions of living with stage four cancer."

Jade first suffered with a cough in 2020, which she visited her GP about, but it was put down to Covid several times. She developed a hoarse voice over the course of 2021 and continued visiting her GP, but once again was reassured she was okay.

‌



By April 2022 she had noticed some other symptoms - nausea, fatigue and swollen lymph nodes. This time, she was referred for a CT scan at Watford General Hospital and was diagnosed with lung cancer, which was present in both lungs.

She said: "The original tumour at that point was 6cm, but there were tumours in both lungs. You never hear about young people who have never smoked getting lung cancer."

The official diagnosis was ALK-positive lung cancer - meaning it is characterised by a mutation in the ALK gene. She didn't need chemotherapy - but was given a daily oral cancer drug to target the specific mutation, which worked successfully - allowing her to go back to work and live a relatively normal life. That was until December 2023, when a check-up scan revealed 17 lesions in her brain.

‌



View 4 Images Jade with her husband Russell (Image: Jade Fardon/SWNS)

She said: "I had been at home getting ready to go out for the evening, volunteering as a Brownie leader, when I got the call."

Jade underwent gamma knife therapy - a targeted radiation therapy - in January 2024, with the aim of 'zapping' the lesions away. Initially it appeared to be successful, but by December 2024, Jade fell unwell with headaches, nausea and sickness and doctors discovered one lesion of the 17 had progressed, despite the gamma knife therapy, causing a brain bleed.

‌



Just before Christmas she underwent brain surgery to remove that lesion at National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, Queen Square, which was successful. But by early April 2025, she once again began feeling unwell, suffering with headaches and nausea, which she put down to migraines and took time off work sick.

On her way to volunteer at Brownies, she had a seizure, phoned 999 and was rushed to A&E. She was extremely unwell for two weeks after scans revealed progression of another lesion in her brain.

She was taken off her original oral medication and given a new one to take, which has since helped slow progression. After one further gamma knife treatment earlier this year, Jade is now being monitored with MRI and CT scans every four months and has opted to move her care to the private sector.

‌



View 4 Images Jade couldn't shift her cough, but doctors put it down to Covid and reassured her it would go away on its own (Image: Jade Fardon/SWNS)

She is able to work four days a week alongside two-monthly oncologist check-ups and her scans. Jade is determined that she won't let her stage four diagnosis hold her back. She is raising awareness and funds for ALK Positive UK, a charity for ALK-positive lung cancer patients, by completing Chris Hoy's charity cycle, Tour De 4, in September.

Jade said: "I'm passionate about challenging assumptions of living with stage four incurable cancer. I didn't used to like telling people I have stage four cancer - now I like to show people what I'm doing. If you have the determination, passion and the right perspective and have the right people around you, you can do anything."

Article continues below

Jade's fundraiser is on GoFundMe.

News.title: Jump in energy bills drives UK inflation to highest rate for four months
News.content:
Higher energy bills drove UK inflation up to 2.9% in the 12 months to July, the latest figures show.

Gas prices rose at the highest rate in almost four years, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, which led to an increase to the energy price cap in July. Energy prices surged after US-Iran war began in February, which has restricted global oil supplies.

It is the highest rate of inflation since March, but some price rises have slowed: food inflation, at 1.3%, is at its lowest rate for close to five years.

Experts say Wednesday's inflation figure is unlikely to influence the Bank of England to change its key interest rate at its next meeting in September.

Energy costs rose on 1 July after regulator Ofgem increased the price cap on household gas and electricity bills by 13%, which added Â£221 a year to the typical household's bill.

Energy bills are forecast to rise by 4% from October, according to Cornwall Insight, which could see bills rise to their highest level since July 2023.

The independent energy consultancy increases are being driven by ongoing uncertainty over the US-Iran conflict, which has seen effective closures of the Strait of Hormuz, a key trading passage for oil-carrying ships.

Cornwall Insight added that energy price pressures were being compounded by the ongoing heatwave across Europe, "increasing gas demand for power generation to meeting air conditioning and cooling demand".

News.title: Burnham unveils plan to get rough sleepers off streets for Christmas
News.content:
In an opinion piece in the Guardian, external, Burnham wrote: "For decades, Westminster has treated rough sleeping like a problem to step around rather than solve. It's a philosophy that took hold in the 1980s and came back full force in the era of austerity: this idea that rough sleeping is just a fact of life rather than something government has a responsibility to end...

"No matter who they are or what they've been through, every person sleeping rough deserves a chance to get back on their feet â and, together, that's exactly what we'll give them."

The prime minister said he wanted to build on the success of Everyone In, a Covid pandemic-era scheme that saw thousands of rough sleepers housed in hotels and temporary accommodation.

About 37,000 people were helped by the scheme following its launch in March 2020. The charity Shelter found that about a quarter of them had found settled accommodation, in the form of housing lasting at least six months., external

The announcement comes with an additional Â£102m in new funding, taking Burnham's total commitment to tackling rough sleeping to Â£442m since becoming prime minister. The money is said to be "fully funded" within the Ministry of Housing's budget.

As well as providing immediate support get people off the streets, the funding is also designed to deliver over 1,000 homes over the next three years to provide rough sleepers with permanent accommodation. The funding will also provide "intensive wraparound support," typically psychiatric and drug and alcohol services to help people rebuild their lives.

Burnham says he will organise a special conference in the autumn, inviting business, charities and faith groups to outline how they can help tackle the problem. Councils and mayors will play a leading role in devising local solutions with the areas with the biggest problem receiving the most support.

Jasmine Basran, head of policy at Crisis, said the charity welcomed the announcement and believed an end to rough sleeping was possible.

"What we also want to see in the longer term is interventions to prevent people from being forced to sleep rough in the first place."

She urged departments across government to work together to address the issue - saying too many people being discharged from hospital or leaving care were ending up on the streets.

Sarah Elliott, Shelter's chief executive, called Burnham's pledge a "game-changing move".

She said "tackling the most visible form of homelessness is a strong start" but urged the prime minister to act on his promise to build more council houses to help people living in temporary accommodation.

The shadow housing secretary said Burnham had promised to end rough sleeping while Manchester mayor "and failed because he didn't do the hard work necessary".

James Cleverly added that families would fear there would be tax rises unless Labour could "come clean on what other programmes they are cutting to pay for this project".

Liberal Democrat housing spokesperson Gideon Amos said: "Sticking plasters won't fix the homelessness crisis. Without a proper long-term plan, people could simply find themselves back on the streets once the festive headlines fade."

He urged Burnham to commit to a Lib Dem target to build 150,000 social homes every year.

Deputy Reform UK leader Richard Tice also criticised Burnham's efforts to tackle homelessness while Manchester mayor, and described the government's new plans as "yet another vague announcement with no substances which uses our most vulnerable for political point-scoring".

News.title: Tennis player Nick Kyrgios suspended after testing positive for cocaine
News.content:
In a lengthy statement on Instagram, Kyrgios said the last few years of injuries had taken "a huge toll on me, both mentally and physically".

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do," he wrote.

"Coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined.

"None of that excuses what I did."

Kyrgios he would be stepping away from social media and public life for the next 28 days to "focus on getting myself right".

Cocaine is classified as a stimulant and substance of abuse on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list.

Reduced sanctions apply for athletes who test positive for the substance out of competition.

However, Kyrgios' sample was submitted during a tournament in which he played singles, ultimately losing in the first round to Adam Walton.

"I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me," Kyrgios added.

"Above all, I'm sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed in myself."

Kyrgios has long been a controversial figure in tennis.

His behaviour on court has been widely criticised and he has been given numerous large fines for smashing racquets, making audible obscenities and arguing with the umpire.

In 2023, he admitted assaulting an ex-girlfriend two years earlier. He avoided a criminal conviction.

He was criticised further for making a series of comments which have been considered misogynistic.

In 2024 he shared a post from controversial influencer Andrew Tate. He later said he had gone "to all lengths" to distance himself from the self-proclaimed misogynist.

Kyrgios was also critical of the handling of two high-profile anti-doping cases involving top players Jannik Sinner and Iga Swiatek, calling them "disgusting" for tennis.

Kyrgios has won seven ATP Tour singles titles and reached the Wimbledon final in 2022, losing in four sets to Novak Djokovic.

He and compatriot Thanasi Kokkinakis won the Australian Open men's doubles title together in 2022.

Kyrgios has also spoken about his struggles with mental health, saying he "genuinely contemplated" suicide and spent time in a psychiatric hospital in London after losing at Wimbledon in 2019.

News.title: Scientists 'stunned' by children's lung recovery in ultra low emission zone
News.content:
Scientists say they have been "stunned" by how quickly young children's lungs began to recover and grow after pollution restrictions were brought in where they lived.

Researchers found that children in London whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution showed impressive improvements after the introduction of an Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) in 2019 reduced emissions.

The study followed more than 3,400 primary school children in London and Luton and provides what scientists believe is the strongest evidence yet that local clean air zones could help reduce some of the harm caused by pollution during childhood.

But independent researchers caution that other factors must also be considered.

Air pollution can stunt the growth of young children's lungs leaving them at an increased risk of asthma, heart disease, diabetes and even premature death.

Children are also more vulnerable to pollution because their lungs and immune systems are still developing. And when outside, they tend to be closer to the ground and nearer sources of exhaust fumes, for example.

In 2020 Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, a nine-year-old girl from London who died following an asthma attack in 2013, became the first person in the UK to have air pollution listed as a cause of death.

In the study, researchers recruited six to nine-year-olds attending primary schools in London's ultra low emission zone and followed the same children for five years, comparing them to similar children (in terms of socio-economic background, physical activity and ethnicity) in Luton.

Children in the study had annual lung function and capacity tests in the year before Ulez came in and for four years after.

Initial results showed children's lungs in London were smaller in capacity than those in Luton, which is less polluted than London but has a similar mix of pollutants.

At the end of the study the children's lung capacity reached near identical levels in both groups.

"While we would expect children's lungs to grow year on year, our results indicate that the London children's lung growth had accelerated during the four years to 'catch up' with the control group in Luton to reach similar levels of lung capacity," researchers say.

"I was absolutely stunned when I first saw the results," Prof Chris Griffiths, a senior author on the study, at Queen Mary University of London, told the BBC.

"The speed of catch up in lung capacity in the London group was surprising and impressive.

"This shows an ambitious clean air zone can drive pollution levels down, rapidly restoring children's stunted lung growth."

The main test measured how much air a child could forcibly breathe out in one second after a big breath in.

In practical terms the improvements could mean children in the London group could run as fast as the Luton group without getting out of breath or blow out the same number of candles for example, Griffiths explained.

Another way of testing for lung capacity used in the study showed significant improvements too, though not to the same extent - implying there are still gains to be made.

Overall the proportion of children in London whose lung capacity was deemed "clinically impaired" (suggesting lung damage resulting in coughs or breathlessness) fell from 14% to 9%.

In Luton - where some smaller scale measures were put in place to tackle air pollution - the figures were 9% to 7%.

The team's measurements also showed the level of nitrogen dioxide children were exposed to fell faster in London than in Luton over this time.

Researchers say this is key as it likely demonstrates that the improved lung growth they saw was related to air quality improvements following the implementation of Ulez.

London's Ulez was first introduced in 2019 by Mayor Sadiq Khan in a bid to "clean up London's air". London had high levels of the harmful gas nitrogen dioxide which comes from motor vehicles.

Older, more polluting vehicles had to pay a daily charge to drive in central London. The measures were later expanded to cover the whole capital. While many supported the policy it provoked political opposition and protests.

News.title: Demand for degree apprenticeships in England quadruples in three years
News.content:
Competition for degree apprenticeships in England has quadrupled over the past three years, the BBC has found.

The popularity of degree apprenticeships - which offer a paid-for university degree along with a salary - has grown as the cost of university has come under increased scrutiny.

Data seen by the BBC showed the number of applicants through the government's central platform nearly tripled from 8,100 to 21,800 over the past three years, while the number of positions available fell by almost half, from 7,300 to 3,700.

Applicants said they applied to university as a "backup" because competition was so fierce, with employers cutting back on hiring because of high employment costs and economic uncertainty.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it was "backing employers who take on young apprentices".

Last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure teenagers had technical routes into careers that could rival the path of a university degree.

His comments came as concerns grow about the immediate and long-term costs of university, with more students wanting to commute from home to save money and calls to reform student loan repayments.

Degree apprenticeships might look to some like an attractive alternative, but the Freedom of Information data obtained by the BBC suggests they are hard to come by.

News.title: Camilla admits it was 'difficult' to keep King's cancer diagnosis a secret
News.content:
Queen Camilla has spoken for the first time about the pressure of keeping King Charles III's cancer diagnosis secret in the early stages of treatment.

In a video to mark the 30th anniversary of Maggie's cancer charity, the Queen, who is president of the charity, recalls how "difficult" it was to avoid discussing her husband's treatment while on an official engagement with cancer patients and their families.

In January 2024, the Queen opened a new Maggie's cancer support centre at the Royal Free Hospital in London.

She had just found out that the King had cancer and would need treatment but had to hold back from telling anyone as the official announcement had not been made public.

"Nobody could say anything at the time, that was quite difficult.

"I almost said something but, you know, I felt that it wasn't the time to say," the Queen told the chief executive of Maggie's, Dame Laura Lee.

"It was just a week before it became public and the courage that must have taken for you," Dame Laura told the Queen - referring to how personally challenging the hospital visit must have been.

"I was just longing to let it out, but obviously I couldn't," the Queen said.

The King's cancer diagnosis was revealed on 5 February 2024, just days after the Queen's engagement at the Royal Free Hospital.

More than two years later, he is still receiving cancer treatment. Buckingham Palace has reiterated that his health continues to move in a "positive direction".

In the seven-minute film recorded at Clarence House, the Queen says the King's way of coping has always been to push on with official duties. She spoke of helping to look after her "poor husband".

"Nothing stopped him. He just said, 'This is my way. I'm going to cope with it,'" she said.

During the hospital visit, the Queen described feeling aware that she was now sharing the experience of so many families she met.

"I was almost questioning them. I didn't want to pry too deeply. But normally when I went in, I was just talking to them, but I don't know, I felt it was much more deep," the Queen said.

"I looked at everybody who was suffering and all the relations and I think it made me realise even more how important these places were."

The King has never disclosed the type of cancer he has, but has engaged widely with those treating and supporting cancer patients.

Maggie's says the King's public announcement prompted a 12% increase in men contacting them with a cancer diagnosis.

"The King's openness about his diagnosis has undoubtedly helped others to be more open themselves, and to now hear the Queen's completely understandable and natural response as a wife shines a light on why it is so important that family and friends also get the support they need," said Dame Laura.

"To hear her speak so powerfully of her own emotions when visiting the Royal Free centre, while knowing about his Majesty's diagnosis, is a huge honour."

Maggie's has 27 centres across the UK, built in the grounds of major NHS cancer hospitals, and supports hundreds of thousands of people each year.

News.title: Rain arrives for some but is another UK heatwave on the way in September?
News.content:
While wet weather is forecast for many this week, some long-range forecasts are suggesting further dry and sunny spells in September.

Many of us have experienced the first bit of rain in around two months as the weather turned more unsettled on Tuesday.

This change in weather patterns will also bring lower temperatures through this week, perhaps falling to around 2 to 4C below the mid-August average.

The prospect of cooler weather has led to speculation about the possibility of another heatwave - the sixth of the year - developing in September.

News.title: Deaf patient given wrong jab due to sign language error, report says
News.content:
A deaf woman was given the wrong vaccine because she was not provided with a British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter at her doctor's surgery, a report says.

The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) said disabled people were being let down by inaccessible communications.

It said the patient, Samantha, had booked a flu jab but was instead given a Covid vaccine after staff failed to show her a BSL video which would have highlighted the error. She said the experience had had a "profound impact" on her.

The Department of Health and Social Care said the "deeply upsetting stories" were "completely unacceptable" and NHS and social care organisations had a duty to make services accessible.

The PHSO investigates complaints about UK government departments, public organisations and the NHS in England.

It said public services were legally required to support people with their accessible communication needs, which might be due to a disability, neurodivergence or English not being their first language.

Samantha had booked her flu and Covid jabs for separate weeks and showed a nurse a note on her phone which said she was there for the "flu jab only", the PHSO said.

Despite that, the practice said it believed it had correctly established Samantha wanted the Covid vaccine and had got her consent through her grandmother, even though she had early-stage dementia and was not in the treatment room.

Following an investigation, the PHSO recommended the surgery should apologise and pay Samantha Â£450. It has also since signed a contract with a sign language interpreting company.

The NHS Northamptonshire Integrated Care Board said it was "very sorry" about Samantha's experience, and that it expected practices to make "reasonable adjustments to support effective communication".

The PHSO said it had found disabled people risked not getting vital information about their healthcare, finances or employment because of a lack of accessible formats such as large print or audio materials.

Since April 2020, it said it had concluded 623 investigations related to reasonable adjustments, of which 496 were upheld or partly upheld.

The report also highlighted the case of Alan Graham, who was deaf and was being treated for cancer at University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Trust.

When an interpreter was not available, hospital staff asked his teenage grandson to interpret for the family and tell Graham's deaf daughter that he might die.

News.title: First giant tuna caught off Yorkshire since 1960s
News.content:
Atlantic bluefin tuna have been caught off the coast of Yorkshire for the first time in an estimated 60 years.

The giant fish had not been seen in the North Sea since the 1960s due to overfishing and the depletion of herring shoals, according to researchers from the University of Exeter who have now tagged six off Whitby.

On Sunday, the five-person crew on board The Dominator landed a whopping 338kg specimen before repeating the feat a day later with a fish that weighed "just a little bit" less, according to crew member Jack Gardner.

"I have never caught anything like it," said the 28-year-old from the village of Paull, near Hull, describing it as the "best feeling ever".

Gardner, who has been on board The Dominator since 2018, said the crew had been about 10 miles (16km) from Whitby Harbour on Sunday when they made their first catch.

"It jumped out of the water, we all just looked at each other in awe," he said.

"We couldn't believe that we had actually hooked into one."

The crew had travelled to an area where they had heard the migratory species had been.

"Just as we were heading home we spotted a group of birds, so we went to try and have a look around there and that's when we hooked into one," said Gardner.

"We knew they were in the waters, it was just whether we could catch them or not because they are fast fish."

The crew dragged the fish for about five miles (8km) before they were able to get it aboard.

"The fight was a lot harder than I thought, the power of it," said Gardner.

Last year a 210kg bluefin tuna caught in waters on the south-wet coast fetched more than Â£2,000 at auction.

Gardner said the rare catch for his crew had already sold before the boat had arrived back in Whitby.

The following day they caught another bluefin tuna which also weighed more than 300kg.

The buyer, Lance Varrell from Hook to Plate, said the fish were "good quality" and would be sold on to restaurants, sushi markets and directly to customers.

"Bluefin tuna is very popular. It's a very premium fish - they call it the Rolls Royce of the sea," he added.

Itamaes (Japanese chefs) based in London would pay as much as Â£100 per kilo "if it's really good", he added.

Gardner said he was "immensely proud" of his crewmates Ben Shutt, Liam Crosby and their apprentice Ada, as well as skipper Clive Easton, for their role in the historic - and fruitful - catch.

News.title: Ovarian cancer and menopause at 19 mean I can't have kids, but it's changed me for the better
News.content:
Enlli started experiencing problems in 2024.

"My periods were changing, I was experiencing severe pain, but I was still being told I was fine," she said.

She described being "completely at a loss" and felt like she was "losing the plot".

But the pain became too much, and she visited A&E at Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor.

Scans revealed what was believed to be a cyst in her pelvic area, and she was placed on a medical plan to carefully monitor her condition, while continuing to work as a trainee mechanic.

"I was taking painkillers and working through the pain," Enlli said.

She then received a call from the hospital to return for further scans, and admitted: "My mind went straight to cancer."

Her worst fears were confirmed, and she was told she had stage 3 ovarian cancer, , externalwhich meant it had spread beyond the pelvis.

"Being told that I wouldn't be able to have my own children, I broke down and cried," she said.

"I had so much support, but it was so difficult hearing those words."

But Enlli said: "In a strange way I was kind of relieved when they told me I had cancer.

"Just because then I had an answer, I had a treatment plan, I was going to get better."

Enlli received fertility treatment, and seven of her eggs were frozen.

She finished chemotherapy in September 2025, and passed her driving test a week later.

Enlli now experiences hot flushes, brain fog, joint and muscle pain and fatigue, and says it can be hard to identify which are from the menopause or effects of the chemotherapy.

"My memory is absolutely awful," she said.

News.title: Suspended Reform UK member vows to fight to remain in party
News.content:
Political commentator Tim Montgomerie has told BBC Newsnight he will fight his suspension from Reform UK for criticising senior party figures in media interviews.

He said his appeal against suspension would be a test case of whether Reform could tolerate free speech.

The party said Montgomerie had been suspended in line with its rules after public criticism he made.

Montgomerie is a right-of-centre political commentator who defected from the Conservatives to Reform UK in 2024, and who has seen himself as a critical friend of the party leadership.

But it seems he is now regarded as more of a critic and less of a friend - and has had his party membership suspended.

On Friday, Montgomerie had told the BBC he was frustrated by party leader Nigel Farage's "aggrieved tone" after last week's Clacton by-election.

And on a Spectator podcast on Tuesday, he had said another senior party figure, Zia Yusuf, needed to become a team player and should not act "like a child" in politics.

It is understood his suspension came after the podcast was recorded but before it was released.

"I am going to fight this suspension. I want to stay in Reform. I didn't leave the Conservative Party lightly," he told Newsnight.

"I think Reform can reach parts of the country that the Conservative Party never will be able to so I'm going to fight my corner in Reform and I'm going to make this a test case of whether it is a party that can tolerate free speech and dissent," he added.

Montgomerie said he supported Reform's policies on immigration and welfare, but he has also highlighted internal tensions in the party.

In a video statement on X after news of his suspension emerged on the Guido Fawkes website, Montgomerie said he was only trying to make the party "better and stronger" with his public criticisms.

He added that Farage did not know about the decision to suspend him, and he had warned the Reform leader when he joined the party that he would be critical at times, as he had been of the Tory leadership when he ran the ConservativeHome website.

Reform's leadership will have to decide whether it is more politically difficult to rescind rather than to retain Montgomerie's party membership.

News.title: Burnham received £345,000 of donations ahead of becoming PM
News.content:
Andy Burnham has registered accepting Â£345,000 of donations over the past year including Â£164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury.

The donations, listed in the most recent version of the MPs' register of interests,, external are the prime minister's first declarations since he was elected to Parliament in June.

Separately, Burnham has also listed hospitality and gifts he received in the year before he returned to Parliament, including trips to Glastonbury, Lancashire Cricket Club and the Aintree Racecourse.

A Labour Party spokesperson said: "It's right that political campaigns are funded by the generous support of party donors, rather than via the public purse.

"All declarations have been made in line with Parliamentary and Electoral Commission rules."

New MPs are required to register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election.

Lord Sainsbury's donations went towards Burnham's campaign to become Labour leader. Businessman Gary Lubner and former Greater Manchester night-time economy tsar Sacha Lord donated Â£25,000 and Â£35,000 to the campaign respectively.

The TV production company Charlie Parsons Creative contributed Â£50,000 and the think tank ThinkLabour, formerly known as Labour Together, provided Â£22,186.

The donations included the provision of office space, IT equipment, staffing, polling, travel, social media support and message testing.

Burnham's list also includes Â£20,000 of donations towards mayoral campaigning from the trade unions Unison, the Communications Workers Union and the Fire Brigades Union.

Labour peer Lord Blunkett appears on the list having donated Â£2,000 towards Burnham's campaign to become the MP for Makerfield.

Gifts and hospitality Burnham accepted when he was mayor of Greater Manchester include:

Four tickets to Glastonbury, where he was speaking at an event, from the festival organisers and Â£1,000 for accommodation from the campaigning group PRS for Music

Tickets worth Â£3,800 to the Brit Awards in Manchester from Sony Music Entertainment

Two tickets worth Â£500 for the Aintree Racecourse from the Jockey Club Racecourse

Two tickets, valued at Â£458, from Lancashire Cricket Club for a game in The Hundred tournament

A hamper basket and Wedgewood tea set worth Â£340 from the ambassador of Qatar

Shortly after becoming prime minister in 2024, Sir Keir Starmer became embroiled in a row over the gifts he had accepted including tickets to a Taylor Swift concert and thousands of pounds for clothes.

He subsequently paid back more than Â£6,000 worth of gifts and hospitality. He also tightened the rules so that serving ministers had to consider "the need to maintain the public's confidence in the standard of propriety" when accepting gifts.

News.title: Join EU migration pact to tackle small boats, says Ed Davey
News.content:
The UK should join the EU's new Migration and Asylum Pact as a way of tackling small boat crossings across the Channel, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey has said.

The agreement, which came into force in June, aims to speed up the asylum process, increase the number of irregular migrants returned to their home countries and spread responsibility for asylum seekers across the EU.

Sir Ed argues that signing up to the pact would allow the UK to return asylum seekers to the first EU country they entered, thereby "destroying the business model" of the gangs behind the crossings.

Labour said the government's efforts to work with European countries to tackle small boat crossings were "bearing fruit".

A Labour spokesperson said more than 47,000 crossings had been prevented in two years and 70,000 people with no right to be in the UK had been removed.

"There's more to do and that will only happen by working in collaboration with the EU," the spokesperson added.

So far this year, more than 14,000 people have arrived in the UK by small boat - a fall of 43% compared to the previous year.

The EU's new pact, which was nearly 10 years in the making, introduces mandatory screening and an updated database to track those arriving in the bloc.

Under the rules, EU nations must take in migrants from those member states that see the highest number of arrivals - such as Italy and Greece - or instead provide extra funding or resources.

News.title: Mobile payments on the rise but cash decline slows
News.content:
Consumers are increasingly relying on their mobile phone to make payments rather than carrying bank cards, new data shows.

Two-thirds of adults in the UK were registered with at least one mobile payment service last year, according to an annual report by banking trade body UK Finance.

Use of a phone to pay has jumped in recent years. It is a decade since Apple Pay was launched in the UK.

While cash use continues to decline, the data suggests that the fall is slowing and that notes and coins will remain an important payment option for many people a decade from now.

Consumers are increasingly storing card details on phones or watches and making contactless payments backed up by facial or fingerprint verification, instead of pressing in a PIN.

Nine in 10 users of mobile wallets have their debit card loaded as their default payment method on their phone, with the remainder having registered their credit card.

News.title: Fire engulfs London waste centre
News.content:
A fire involving 50 tonnes of household waste has "severely damaged" a recycling facility in south-east London.

Fifteen fire engines were called to Landmann Way in South Bermondsey shortly before 20:00 BST on Monday.

London Fire Brigade (LFB) said the fire was brought under control just after 02:00 on Wednesday, with crews remaining on scene to extinguish pockets of fire.

The LFB said the cause of the fire was not yet known. Firefighters tackled a blaze at the same facility in June.

Speaking from the scene, station commander Duncan Rees said: "Crews worked hard in difficult conditions to bring the fire under control."

He added that ladders were used to tackle the flames from above.

News.title: British couple on honeymoon killed in helicopter crash on Greek island
News.content:
A young British couple and their pilot were killed in a helicopter crash on the Greek island of Sifnos on Monday, Greek police have said.

They have been named as newlyweds Alexander Cromie and Marie Ebert, who were in Greece on their honeymoon.

The private Bell 206 helicopter crashed just metres from a landing pad, killing the pair and their pilot, a Greek national.

The couple are said to have taken the helicopter from the village of Markopoulo near Athens to the popular holiday island, Kathimerini reported.

Greece's aviation safety authority told the BBC it was investigating the crash and that its investigators were heading to the scene on Tuesday to gather evidence and speak to witnesses.

News.title: Viral pastry craze causes huge queues in the Dolomites
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A mountain hut in the Italian Dolomites has been overwhelmed by tourists after viral videos of a traditional pastry were shared on social media.

The Friedrich August hut in Val di Fassa sits 2,300 metres above sea level and serves homemade krapfen, a traditional doughnut-like pastry, during peak season.

Influencer videos of the €3 (£2.57) krapfen have prompted hordes of hikers to line up at the Italian refuge before the freshly baked goods run out.

The hut’s website warns visitors not to miss their “vanilla-cream-filled krapfen doughnuts, which you can enjoy while sitting and soaking up the view of Mt Sassolungo” in the summer months from 7.30am.

open image in gallery Krapfen, a traditional doughnut-like German pastry ( Getty Images )

Footage shared on TikTok shows snaking queues of up to 300 people waiting to try the pastry.

One blogger wrote: “Honestly didn’t expect a doughnut at 2,300 meters to taste this good. But the homemade krapfen at Rifugio Friedrich August are something special. Freshly made, still warm, paired with a great coffee and an incredible view of the Sassolungo and Sasso Piatto… that’s hard to beat.”

Another said: “The 20-minute hike starts from Passo Sella; I’d start as early as possible as it gets busy (I got there at 7.30am and by the time I left at 8.30am there were queues.”

Overtourism is becoming an increasing problem in the Dolomites.

Last summer, Italian farmers tried to tackle overtourism by charging visitors a fee for hiking on a public footpath.

Four farmers set up a turnstile on the Seceda mountain, a popular place to visit for pictures of the striking Odle Peaks.

At the turnstile, visitors had to pay €5 (£4.32) per person for access to the path.

President of the Italian Alpine Club Francesco Abbruscato told Vita.it: “Until five or six years ago, we didn't see overtourism in certain parts and specific moments of the Dolomites. Now there are iconic places where it's no longer possible to appreciate the beauty, surrounded by dozens of people taking selfies and who are there just for that.”

News.title: Girl fights for her life in hospital after three family members die in beach tragedy
News.content:
Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the world Sign up to our free Morning Headlines email Sign up to our free Morning Headlines email Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A girl is fighting for her life in hospital after three of her family members died after getting into trouble in the water off Shoreham-by-Sea.

Emergency services were called on Tuesday afternoon following reports of four people in difficulty in the open water, Sussex Police have said.

Several ambulances and two air ambulances were seen near the RNLI station in Shoreham-by-Sea, West Sussex, on Tuesday afternoon.

It is thought the four family members went into the sea for a swim.

Sussex Police confirmed on Tuesday night that a man, a woman and a teenage girl had died, while a younger girl from the family was in a critical condition in hospital.

open image in gallery People watch after three people got into difficulty at Shoreham-by-Sea (Jamie Lashmar/PA) ( PA Wire )

Officers have not named the victims but said their next of kin had been informed and were being supported by specialist officers.

Joss Loader, who lives nearby and represents Shoreham Beach Residents’ Association on Adur District Council, said: “There’s just a really strong sense of shock, obviously people are really concerned for the young girl.

“A small tightly knight community with a very deep sense of shock and that sense of disbelief you get after a tragedy because it has come out of nowhere.”

Shoreham Beach is a spit of land with water on three sides from the River Adur, the estuary and the sea, and Ms Loader said the “tragic events” happened in the estuary.

“It’s school holidays and we have had a wonderful summer so the beaches have been packed with families,” she said.

“The weather was quite calm, not as hot as recent days but it was a perfectly normal day.

open image in gallery There was a huge emergency service response to the incident (Jamie Lashmar/PA) ( PA Wire )

“People swim from those beaches even in the winter, generally it is considered as safe as the sea can be. You wouldn’t be swimming there and think you were taking a risk.”

Speaking to reporters, Chief Superintendent James Collis said: “Around 2:40 pm this afternoon, emergency services were called to reports of four people in difficulty in the water close to Shoreham Fort.

“Sussex Police supported His Majesty’s Coast Guard and the RNLI as all four people were brought to shore.

“Tragically, despite the best efforts of paramedics, three people – a man, a woman, and a teenage girl – were sadly confirmed deceased.

“A younger girl has been taken to hospital and is in critical condition. We can confirm all four people were from the same family, and their next of kin have been informed.”

The A259 Brighton Road was blocked in both directions from New Road to Kingston Lane because of the incident.

A resident, who asked to remain anonymous, told The Telegraph: “I heard from friends in the coastguard that it was a family who had been living in tents by the harbour front.

“They were camping just between the harbour arm and the fort. They have been there for a couple weeks, I’ve walked my dog past them. People don’t usually camp there.”

Alan Facer, a fisherman from Hove, told the newspaper: “The wind earlier was south-westerly so usually the waves pick up quite a bit.

“At 3pm, the tide would have been quite high.

“I was thinking the other day that someone is going to get hurt around here.”

open image in gallery An air ambulance lands on the beach at Shoreham-by-Sea ( PA Wire )

Shoreham-by-sea is a coastal town outside of Brighton, and is a popular spot for families and day-trippers heading to the beach.

Water sports are popular from its shingle beach, including paddleboarding and kitesurfing, while parts of the harbour and port areas are used for industrial purposes.

An RNLI spokesman said: “Shoreham RNLI were tasked by HM Coastguard at approximately 3pm on Tuesday 18 August.”

At the scene, an ambulance could be seen leaving under a police escort with blue lights flashing.

An HM Coastguard spokesperson added: “HM Coastguard responded to an incident reported at Shoreham at about 2.45pm on 18 August.

“An HM Coastguard helicopter was sent as well as Littlehampton, Shoreham and Newhaven Coastguard Rescue Teams, and an RNLI lifeboat from Shoreham.

“Sussex Police and South East Coast Ambulance Service also attended.”

The South East Coast Ambulance Service also said they were responding to reports that four people needed medical attention after getting into difficulty in the water near Shoreham Harbour.

open image in gallery A younger girl from the same family is in a critical condition ( PA )

“We were called shortly after 3pm and have a number of ambulance resources at the scene,” a spokesperson said.

“We have no further information to share at this time but will provide updates as soon as possible.”

East Worthing and Shoreham MP Tom Rutland said in a statement on Facebook: “I am deeply saddened by the tragic news that three people have died following an incident in the water near Shoreham Fort this afternoon.

“I spoke earlier with Sussex Police and Shoreham RNLI and have been briefed on the response by the emergency services.

“My thoughts are with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives, and I know the whole community here in Shoreham will be hoping and praying for the recovery of the young girl receiving medical treatment in hospital.”

News.title: Ex-Fauci adviser pleads guilty to conspiracy to hide Covid-19 origins research
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A former senior adviser to infectious disease expert Dr. Anthony Fauci pleaded guilty Tuesday to plotting to conceal federal records related to research on the origins of the deadly Covid-19 pandemic.

Dr. David Morens, who had worked under Fauci as a senior official at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) during the pandemic, entered his plea to a conspiracy charge during a hearing in federal court in Greenbelt, Maryland.

Morens pleaded guilty to conspiring to defraud the U.S. government, a felony punishable by a maximum prison sentence of five years. He is scheduled to be sentenced 12 November by U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis.

“By pleading guilty today, Dr. Morens has taken responsibility for what he did, and he will continue to do so," defense attorney Tim Belevetz said in a statement after the plea hearing.

Dr. Morens is accused of using his private email account to intentionally circumvent public records laws. ( Getty )

Morens is accused of using his private email account to intentionally circumvent public records laws while employed at NIAID. The Justice Department alleges that he concealed or destroyed records of discussions related to COVID-19 research grants, including an effort to revive a controversial coronavirus grant.

The indictment follows a probe by House Republicans into the origins of the Covid-19 pandemic that scrutinized Morens’ email communications and accused him of intentionally concealing records. In congressional testimony, Morens denied attempting to evade federal transparency laws by using his personal email.

In July, Fauci repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination during a congressional hearing on his handling of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Last Friday, Fauci declined a request to appear voluntarily before a second Senate panel after majority Republicans on the Homeland Security Committee voted along partisan lines to hold him in contempt of Congress.

Fauci wasn't charged in the case against Morens, 78, of Chester, Maryland.

Additional reporting by Reuters.

News.content:
Trump casts doubt on Iran deal, says Tehran ‘cannot have a nuclear weapon’

Iran has threatened to target any Gulf states assist the US in the conflict, following a report that it could target American military assets in Europe if Trump were to escalate the conflict.

“Nothing is hidden from our eyes”, Iran’s army chief Ali Abdollahi said, adding: “We warn: Any assistance and facilitation to the aggressive US army is tantamount to participation with the US military forces.”

It comes after Iranian regime insiders told The Financial Times that Tehran could target US military assets in Europe if Donald Trump escalates the conflict, as the US president claimed the Strait of Hormuz as American territory.

Tehran has considered strikes on US targets in south-eastern Europe, including Bulgaria, which last month approved the use of its Bezmer air base by US refuelling aircraft, the two insiders said.

Cyprus has also been identified as a potential target, one of the insiders said. A British air base on the island was struck by a drone in March.

It came as Trump said there were “no talks or conversation” going on or scheduled with Iran. Calling Hormuz as “New US territory” he shared a crude map of the region with a large blue circle over Hormuz.

News.title: Should you book your flu vaccine now? Expert advice as NHS opens appointments
News.content:
Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the world Sign up to our free Morning Headlines email Sign up to our free Morning Headlines email Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

The NHS is urging millions of people to book their flu jabs early ahead of the winter rush.

Flu season may seem like months away, but the health service is starting preparations earlier by opening its booking system to eligible people, including pregnant people and children.

The NHS has had to treat record numbers of patients this summer amid five back-to-back heatwaves.

It now wants to do everything it can to ease winter demands.

In 2025, nearly 19 million people received their flu jab in England, and around 104,000 hospitalisations are estimated to have been avoided as a result.

Here are all the details on who is eligible for a free flu vaccine and the optimal time to get it.

open image in gallery Those over the age of 65, pregnant people, and those with certain health conditions are all eligible for a free flu jab (file photo) ( PA Wire )

How to get a flu jab

Certain eligible groups can get a free NHS flu vaccine. These are people who:

are aged 65 or over

have certain long-term health conditions

are pregnant

live in a care home

are the main carer for an older or disabled person, or receive a carer's allowance

live with someone who has a weakened immune system

Anyone eligible who wants to book a flu jab can: contact their GP surgery to book an appointment; book at a pharmacy online or in the NHS App; or find a pharmacy that offers free NHS flu vaccination.

Those who are not eligible for a free NHS jab but still want to receive a vaccination can pay for a private service. This is offered at pharmacies like Boots and Superdrug, usually for around £20.

When do flu vaccinations start?

Vaccinations start on 1 September and run through to March.

Flu season usually peaks in December and January, so the NHS is starting vaccinations in autumn, to ensure those at risk are protected and fewer people are hospitalised.

Local NHS services will begin sending invites to the first cohort of people eligible – children and pregnant women – next month via their GP practice, NHS app or letter.

Other cohorts will begin receiving the jab from 1 October. These include those aged 65 years and over, all adults in a clinical risk group, and adults in care homes, carers and people in close contact with the immunocompromised and frontline healthcare workers.

This year’s cohort includes adults aged 75 years and over, residents in a care home for older adults, and individuals aged 6 months and over who are immunosuppressed.

open image in gallery Flu vaccination will start from September for pregnant women and children ( Getty/iStock )

How long does it take for the flu vaccine to take effect?

The flu vaccine takes about two weeks to reach peak effectiveness.

That’s because the immune system needs time to produce the protective antibodies against the influenza viruses in the vaccine.

But the vaccine offers protection for about three months.

Ideally, patients should get the vaccine at the start of winter so they are protected before getting exposed to the winter flu.

Why you should get the flu vaccine

Although getting a flu jab doesn’t stop a flu infection, it does reduce the chance of severe illness. It also reduces the chance of passing the flu on to someone else who is vulnerable.

Chief nursing officer for England Duncan Burton said: “The NHS is kicking off its preparations for winter earlier than ever, with millions of flu jab appointments for pregnant women and children available to book from today ahead of vaccinations starting next month.

“The flu jab is one of our best defences against winter illness. It takes just a few minutes, but it can protect you for months, helping to prevent serious illness, avoid hospital admissions and keep the most vulnerable people.”

News.title: Household energy bills expected to jump to three-year high in October
News.content:
For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Household energy prices are set increase again to the highest level for three years heading into winter, according to new forecasts.

Bills are due to increase despite the Prime Minister’s plan to remove VAT from household electricity bills from October.

The energy price cap is currently expected to increase by 4% in October compared with the current rate, experts at Cornwall Insight said.

Analysts said the increase is driven by continued uncertainty linked to the Middle East conflict, which has pushed wholesale energy prices higher.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham is removing VAT from electricity bills for six months from October (Finnbarr Webster/PA) ( PA Wire )

The ongoing heatwaves across Europe have added further pressure by increasing gas demand for power generation to meet air conditioning and cooling demand.

Cornwall said it expected a typical household to be facing an annual bill of £1,729, up from £1,663, based on an Ofgem’s updated definition of a typical consumer, which came into effect from July to reflect falling household energy use.

It said this would be the equivalent of £1,941 per year based on its previous calculations, up from £1,862 currently.

It would mark the highest average bill since July 2023.

The increased October cap, which will remain in place for three months, will come into force as households start to increase their energy usage further by using their heating more regularly, adding to bills.

Cornwall said the expected increase in October will be less than otherwise expected because of the proposed removal of VAT from household electricity bills.

The Prime Minister previously said this would knock around £45 off the annual Ofgem price cap from October.

However, the experts said the recent swing in global energy prices has more than offset the downward impact of the VAT policy.

Dr Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, said: “Rising energy bills aren’t welcome at the best of times, but with winter approaching this latest hike will hit struggling households especially hard.

“Driven by international conflict rather than domestic policy, it is a stark reminder that our energy bills remain tied to events thousands of miles away.

“Moments like this are the strongest argument for reducing Britain’s reliance on volatile international gas.

“While temporary relief like VAT cuts help soften the blow, they don’t touch the underlying fact that Britain is heavily dependent on imports of natural gas.”

A Government spokesman said: “Tackling the cost of living remains a key priority for this Government and we know families will be worried by the prospect of higher energy bills this winter.

“We’re acting to give consumers breathing space with the cost of living – cutting VAT on energy bills, ensuring around six million households get the £150 warm home discount this winter, and making millions of homes cheaper to run through our warm homes plan.

“Alongside our efforts to support rapid de-escalation in the Middle East, we will do everything we can to shield consumers from global energy shocks and bring down bills for good.”

News.title: Before-and-after Nasa images show crater carved by a SpaceX rocket that slammed into the Moon
News.content:
Sign up to our free weekly IndyTech newsletter delivered straight to your inbox Sign up to our free IndyTech newsletter Sign up to our free IndyTech newsletter Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

New Nasa images show the best view yet of a crater left behind after a SpaceX rocket crashed into the Moon.

The space agency released before-and-after photos of the impact area, taken from a spacecraft circling the Moon, on Tuesday.

The Falcon rocket’s upper stage plowed into the moon at 5,400 mph (8,700 kph) on Aug. 5 after drifting through space for more than a year. It launched a pair of private moon landers with experiments and even a tiny rover in 2025 as part of NASA’s push to commercialize lunar exploration.

Based on these new photos by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, the fresh crater appears to be 60 feet (18 meters) across and less than 10 feet (3 meters) deep, according to scientists.

Dark and bright streaks are clearly visible emanating like butterfly wings from the crater. The darker lines represent excavated material that was close to the surface and shaped by eons of solar wind, cosmic rays and micrometeorite strikes. The brighter rays indicate fresh rocks and dirt that were hurled from farther down.

The spacecraft photographed the crater a week after the collision from 60 miles (96 kilometers) up, while zooming along at one mile per second. Flight controllers had to tilt the spacecraft so its cameras pointed toward the impact scene.

The orbiter completes a lunar polar orbit every two hours, as the moon rotates beneath. It took six days before the crash scene came into view.

South Korea’s Danuri spacecraft was first on the scene to beam back photos.

The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has been orbiting the moon since 2009, serving as NASA's up-close eyes as the space agency works to return astronauts to the lunar surface.

News.title: Shattered 700-year-old skeleton could be earliest-known victim of popular siege weapon
News.content:
A shattered skeleton found in the ruins of Scotland’s Stirling Castle likely belongs to the world’s earliest-known trebuchet victim, according to a new study.

“Skeleton 150”, as the remains are known, belonged to a man in his 20s who died during a siege of the castle about 700 years ago.

He died from a massive blow that shattered his skull and pinned him to the ground. “While the use of siege engines is well documented, we believe this is the first evidence of trebuchet trauma in the archaeological record,” researchers noted in the study presented at the European meeting of the Paleopathology Association in Berlin last week.

In the study, archaeologists examined nine skeletons unearthed at the Stirling Castle for evidence of trauma related to the Scottish Wars of Independence of 1296-1328 and 1332-1357.

It was during the first war that the castle was besieged in 1304 by Edward I, who utilised siege engines, including the “War Wolf” trebuchet, believed to be the largest such weapon ever made.

Historical records suggest the 300ft tall trebuchet took five master carpenters and 50 labourers three months to build and that it could shoot projectiles as heavy as 140kg.

It was a projectile from such a trebuchet that killed the man behind Skeleton 150, the study found.

open image in gallery Trebuchet ( ChrisO/Wikimedia )

Scientists used radiography, microscopy, and CT X-ray scans to analyse the skeleton and found that it carried 61 fractures to the skull and 57 to the ribs and extensive damage to vertebrae, arms and right shoulder.

“SK150 was notable for having over 160 peri-mortem fractures across his skeleton, from the top of his cranium to his knees,” they said.

Initially, researchers suspected the bones were broken after burial but the latest scans helped confirm the fractures were suffered when the person was alive.

“Detailed analysis indicates this peri-mortem trauma was all blunt force,” they wrote in the study.

open image in gallery Soldiers wearing chain mail load baskets of stones on to a trebuchet behind the walls of a castle circa 1400 ( Getty )

The patterns of the fracture indicated that the trebuchet projectile likely struck the man on his right shoulder and the back of his skull.

“Comparison with known forensic cases indicates this trauma was the result of a single, high-velocity impact, probably to a living individual with forearms flexed in front of the body and bearing weight through the lower limbs and feet,” researchers Jo Buckberry and Patrick Randolph-Quinney noted.

The findings highlight the brutality of medieval warfare and the importance of recording trauma in ancient skeletons.

While the timing of the man’s death and the pattern of his injuries indicated the man was a victim of a War Wolf or similar trebuchet, researchers were unable to confirm this due to the lack of comparable forensic cases from that time period.

News.title: Unemployment rate fails to fall for Burnham
News.content:
An expected drop in the unemployment rate has failed to materialise, dealing a setback to Andy Burnham’s hopes of reviving Britain’s ailing economy.

Unemployment remained stuck at 4.9pc in the three months to June, while the number of payrolled employees fell by 13,000, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics. Economists had predicted that the unemployment rate would ease to 4.8pc.

While the three-month figure was flat, monthly data showed a sharp increase at the end of the period. Unemployment jumped to 5.4pc in June, up from 4.6pc the previous month.

That marked the highest reading since October 2020 and the biggest monthly jump in 13 years.

Julian Jessop, at the Institute of Economic Affairs, described the latest jobs figures as “dire”.

He said: “The unemployment rate remains stubbornly high, with a big jump in the single month figure for June.”

It came as private sector wage growth slumped to a six-year low of just 2.8pc. That stands in contrast to a 6.1pc pay increase for the average public sector worker in the same period.

Meanwhile, vacancies dropped to 707,000 in the three months to July – the lowest level since 2021 – with a particular strain on entry-level job openings.

Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, warned that the UK was “trapped in a deepening jobs drought”.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “Stagnant, or even negative, real wage growth in the second half of this year will intensify the pressure on Burnham and Healey to come up with a package to support the cost of living.

“However, doing anything substantial without breaching either the fiscal rules or the manifesto commitments looks increasingly difficult given the deterioration in headroom and commitments to spend big on everything from defence to social care.”

News.title: Top British scientist steps down from WHO
News.content:
One of Britain’s best-known scientists has resigned as assistant director-general of the World Health Organization.

Sir Jeremy Farrar became a household name during the pandemic when he served on the UK’s Scientific Advisory Group for Emergencies (Sage).

Sources inside the WHO and the broader scientific community told The Telegraph he resigned his position on Monday.

While it is not clear what prompted his resignation, colleagues told The Telegraph he had been unhappy within the organisation for some time. One speculated that he had become increasingly frustrated with its internal politics and bureaucracy.

Sir Jeremy, 64, who was also a former director of the Wellcome Trust, could not immediately be reached for comment.

The surprise move comes at a difficult time for the WHO, which is undergoing a major restructuring after suffering cuts and a massive funding shortfall following the United States’s withdrawal from it in January. It is also fighting a major outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s Director-General, announced Dr Farrar’s decision in an email to all staff on Tuesday morning, saying that the British scientist will “retire” from the WHO, effective September 30.

In the email, seen by The Telegraph, Dr Tedros said: “Dr Farrar has demonstrated an exceptional commitment to science and public health at the highest levels, and we are grateful that he chose to bring his experience, energy and conviction to WHO.

“On behalf of the entire organisation, I extend my sincere thanks to Dr Farrar... [and wish] him every success in his next chapter and a well-deserved retirement.”

He added that Dr Bruce Aylward will take over as the new Assistant Director-General for Health Promotion, Disease Prevention and Care.

News.title: Rabies deaths are rising. What is going wrong?
News.content:
In a packed intensive care ward in Dhaka, three-year-old Abdul lay paralysed, his tiny body contorted by a rabies infection that had reached his brain.

His mother, Sheuli Akter, 38, sat at his side massaging his legs in the hope that this might loosen his muscles, but it was having no effect. Even his hands and feet were seized up by cramps.

Abdul had been in the hospital for a month but doctors said he was unlikely to live much longer. The infection, they said, had progressed to degenerative encephalitis; the virus had got to his brain.

Abdul was shaking, gripped by fever. His breathing was rapid and panicked, punctuated occasionally by groans of pain.

On his chin was the telltale scar of a dog bite, the source of the infection.

“He was playing outside with the other children,” said Sheuli. “The dog, which was one of those always waiting around outside, suddenly attacked him. They said it went for him because he was the smallest.”

News.title: Arsenal hunger is ominous for rivals as they dismantle Man City
News.content:
Was it the early goal that should have put Arsenal’s rivals on red alert? No. While Ricardo Calafiori’s intervention was dramatic, it wasn’t that. Was it the seamless introduction of the new signings, then? No, it wasn’t that either, despite the excellence of Bruno Guimarães and Christos Tzolis.

How about the emphatic scoreline – surely that was it? Again, the answer is no. Three unanswered goals against Manchester City will always grab a headline, but scorelines do not always define the nature of a performance or a team’s capabilities.

So what was it that should have those with pretensions of ripping Arsenal’s crown from their grasp shuffling uncomfortably? One word: hunger. The reason this was such an ominous afternoon for the chasing pack is the fact Mikel Arteta’s team played with intensity of a team with everything to prove.

Title wins can sometimes sate ambition. Players don’t always want to climb the same mountain again, not least if reaching the peak was initially so draining, but everywhere you looked on a day when Cardiff was painted red and white was evidence that Arsenal remain ravenous for success.

First Guimarães pounced out of the shadows to mug Jérémy Doku, leaving him in a heap. Then there was Gabriel Magalhães thundering into a befuddled Doku, celebrating in front of City’s fans as if he had scored, before Ben White flung himself in front of the Belgian, denying a clear-cut scoring opportunity.

News.content:

Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty for the second successive pre-season friendly as Manchester United were beaten 4-2 by former head coach Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan.

Fernandes, who rolled a spot-kick wide in a shoot-out against Leeds in midweek, was gifted the chance to open his pre-season account in Wroclaw, Poland.

His effort was on target this time, but Milan keeper Lorenzo Torriani dived to his right to beat the shot away.

Fernandes did at least get an assist, taking the second-minute corner which was powerfully headed home by Harry Maguire to give United the lead.

Sports.title: New stadium row at heart of Chelsea ownership wrangle as Todd Boehly looks to sell stake
Sports.content:
New stadium row at heart of Chelsea ownership wrangle as Todd Boehly looks to sell stake

Todd Boehly is open to selling his stake in Chelsea just over four years after his arrival at Stamford Bridge and it appears that an argument over the Blues’ stadium is at the centre of his decision

View 2 Images Todd Boehly looks set to sell his stake in Chelsea (Image: Getty Images)

A row over the re-development of Stamford Bridge is reportedly at the heart of Todd Boehly’s decision to leave Chelsea. The American arrived in West London back in May 2022 as part of a £4.25bn takeover to replace Roman Abramovich.

‌



Alongside Clearlake Capital, Boehly’s BlueCo consortium have since poured money into the club, with millions having been spent on transfers, as well as managers.

‌



But it appears that Boehly’s time at the helm is set to come to an end, with reports suggesting that he is looking to cash in on his share in the club following disagreements with co-owner Behdad Eghbali.

‌



According to The Sun, a main sticking point is the redevelopment of the Blues’ Stamford Bridge home. Both Boehly and Eghbali agree that Chelsea need a new, purpose-built venue away from the current site but have different visions.

Neither side is willing to provide their share of the £5bn construction cost, while the other camp would still retain huge influence over the project and direction of the West London club.

‌



Boehly is set to leave his role as Chelsea chairman at the end of the season, which could lead to a natural exit, albeit a deal to buy him out is not expected to be easy.

Speaking about the potential of a new stadium in March last year with Bloomberg, Boehly said: “We have a big stadium development opportunity that we have to figure out. And I think the owners will either be aligned, or we ultimately decide to go our different ways.

“It’s not as if we are building something in the middle of a rural environment. We have a lot of constituencies to consider. Certainly, the Chelsea fan base is one. But long-term, I think we’re going to be building something new, and we’ll figure it out.

‌



“Stadium development is happening around the world. You’re going to see the NBA expanding into Europe, new stadiums and arenas being built. We’re just at the very beginning of this wave, and sporting infrastructure will be a major part of it.”

View 2 Images Chelsea have long had plans in place to redevelop Stamford Bridge (Image: Getty Images)

“We’ve been aligned on what we’re trying to do and what we’re trying to build,” he added. “If you look at the evolution of the team, we’ve been working together on building a young squad with long contracts. That was all new. In order to do what we’ve done, it’s because we’re aligned.”

Chelsea had an eye-catching plan for the redevelopment of Stamford Bridge granted planning permission in January 2017, albeit that was scrapped just over a year later, citing an ‘unfavourable investment climate’.

Aston Villa respond to shock £38m Ollie Watkins bid as Al-Hilal step up transfer pursuit

Al-Hilal are pushing to sign Ollie Watkins from Aston Villa, having reportedly agreed personal terms with the England international before lodging a £38million offer

View 2 Images Ollie Watkins could be moving to Saudi Arabia (Image: Neville Williams/Aston Villa FC via Getty Images)

Aston Villa have rejected a £38million bid for Ollie Watkins from Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal. Watkins, 30, has now been the subject of three offers from Al-Hilal, with personal terms reportedly already in place.

The striker didn't feature in pre-season for Villa and missed last week's UEFA Super Cup clash with Paris Saint-Germain. Watkins was given additional time off following the World Cup alongside Villa team-mates Ezri Konsa and Emiliano Martinez, whose futures are also in doubt.

Villa turned down Al-Hilal's latest proposal on Tuesday night, but the Premier League club braced for yet another improved bid. Unai Emery's side have already lost key players in the form of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne this summer, bringing in a combined £159.5m.

Watkins was the subject of interest from Manchester United and Arsenal last year, while Turkish giants Fenerbahce were keen to sign him earlier this summer before turning their attention to Romelu Lukaku. After being handed a new contract in 2024, Watkins has two years left on his deal at Villa Park.

Despite being England's second-choice striker behind Harry Kane, Watkins only made two appearances at the World Cup. He was given a 12-minute cameo against Panama in the group stage before playing the second half of England's third-place play-off victory over France.
