World.title: Embattled Florida Republican Rep. Cory Mills loses his fight to keep his House seat
World.content:
Embattled Florida Republican Rep. Cory Mills loses his fight to keep his House seat

toggle caption Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

In Florida's primary election, Republican incumbent Rep. Cory Mills lost his race in the 7th congressional district. That's according to a race call by The Associated Press.

Mills, running for his third term, lost to his main Republican challenger, former local television news anchor Ryan Elijah who won by about 12 percentage votes.

Mills is the latest lawmaker in a recent string of congressional members facing scandals and allegations of domestic abuse while running for elected office. The House Ethics Committee opened an investigation this year over allegations that Mills assaulted a former girlfriend and also violated campaign finance laws.

Sponsor Message

NPR reached out to Mills' office for a response to those allegations but did not hear back. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Mills' campaign signs feature "Trump Endorsed" in big letters across the top, and though President Trump did endorse him in February, he left Mills out of a number of endorsements posted on social media running up to Tuesday's primary election.

And when asked about Mills late last week, Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida said, "I have not endorsed Cory Mills, and I do not support Cory Mills."

Mills' campaign website shows the endorsements of about a dozen House Republicans. Meanwhile, his main GOP challenger, former local television news anchor Ryan Elijah, has been endorsed by Florida GOP Reps. Anna Paulina Luna and Mike Haridopolos. Also running in the GOP primary are real estate agent Sarah Ulrich and U.S. Army veteran and Department of Defense employee Michael Don Johnson.

Loading...

The 7th Congressional District is situated in central Florida, from the northern suburbs of Orlando to the coast south of Daytona Beach. It is one of seven districts left unchanged when Florida redrew its congressional maps in May.

Sanford sits in the heart of the district, and it's where resident Patrick Austin cast his ballot over the weekend.

"He delivers for our district," said Austin. "He's brought a lot of money. He's fixed a lot of issues that we needed — that's all I want."

Voter Tiffany Davis said Mills had too much "baggage" for her to vote for him. She is concerned that if he wins the primary, he'll lose in the general election.

"I think Cory Mills is going to get beat, honestly, if it comes to a Democrat, and I just don't think I can chance it," she said. "I think he has a lot of issues. I think he was a good guy, but he has too many issues right now."

The scandals around Mills have muddied Republicans' clear chance of winning and keeping the seat. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report, which tracks races, moved Mills' district from the "solid Republican" column to the less certain "likely Republican."

Sponsor Message

Even though Mills won this district twice, Democrats consider this race competitive and are putting money toward flipping the seat.

Elijah will face Bale Dalton, a 24-year Navy veteran and former NASA chief of staff, who was backed by The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

World.title: ABC and Disney sue FCC, alleging First Amendment violations
World.content:
ABC and Disney sue FCC, alleging First Amendment violations

toggle caption Aurore Marechal/Getty Images

The ABC network sued the Federal Communications Commission in federal court Tuesday in a case with major First Amendment implications, arguing that the Trump administration has violated its free speech rights by launching investigations and challenging its broadcast licenses in retaliation for its news coverage, late-night satire and views on talk shows.

ABC and its corporate parent, The Walt Disney Co., allege that the FCC has taken these actions to appease President Trump, who has repeatedly called for the network to be stripped of its licenses in response to material that has sparked his ire.

Sponsor Message

The network's lawsuit cites Trump's own social media posts, which condemn ABC's news coverage, its talk show The View and late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel, who has frequently mocked the president.

The lawsuit starts: "Government censorship is deeply un-American."

It goes on to note that, in the words of a recent unanimous U.S. Supreme Court decision involving the National Rifle Association, the government may not "use the power of the State to punish or suppress disfavored expression."

"This case concerns the Administration's sustained effort to do just that," the ABC/Disney lawsuit argues. "The Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts."

ABC and Disney own eight local TV stations, which beam out the national network's shows and local programming in specific regions. Among them are stations in six of the United States' largest markets, which contribute significantly to ABC's bottom line.

They require federal licenses because they rely on the public airwaves. The FCC forced all eight of them to undergo early scrutiny of the renewal process of their licenses, years ahead of schedule. It's an essentially unprecedented move in the modern era.

In an interview with NPR on Tuesday evening, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said that Disney and ABC were jumping the gun. He noted that the agency had not yet made any decision about whether to renew the licenses.

Sponsor Message

"Disney seems a little jumpy right now," Carr said. "Disney has chosen to go to court to try to block the FCC from moving forward with respect to at least some of the procedural options that are in front of the agency. But from our perspective, we're going to continue to follow the facts and the law wherever they may lead. Perhaps Disney is concerned or worried about how the record is developing."

"Ultimately, they're going to get a fair shake before the agency," Carr said.

The commission has historically acted in a quasi-independent role from presidential administrations, with the president's party holding three seats and the opposing party two. But Trump publicly said before taking office that he saw the commission as an extension of the executive branch; recent court decisions have reined in the independence of some other semiautonomous agencies set up by Congress; and Carr has acted as a booster and advocate for Trump's excoriation of the press, including ABC.

For his part, Carr has said he is making sure that broadcasters operate in the public interest — a legal requirement — and that they don't violate Trump's executive order on diversity, equity and inclusion.

But he has also been outspoken in his support for Trump's agenda, including specific criticisms of ABC, Kimmel, The View and its journalists. In one instance, he warned that ABC and Disney could "do this the easy way or the hard way" amid the president's call for Kimmel to be pulled off the air. The host was suspended and returned days later after a major public outcry.

Ironically, ABC had been the first in a string of major media companies and digital giants to reach settlements with Trump over lawsuits he filed against them as a private citizen. It paid $16 million to settle his defamation case in December 2024, involving remarks by anchor George Stephanopoulos, after Trump had won a return to the White House but before his inauguration.

Sponsor Message

Given Trump's continuing broadsides against Kimmel, ABC's daytime talk show The View and its journalists, however, Disney has taken an increasingly assertive stance against the administration.

"We're very principled on this," Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told CNBC's Julia Boorstin last week. "We're going to stand up to what we believe is journalistic integrity, and we're not going to be told how to run that side of our business."

He took over from former Disney Chairman and CEO Bob Iger in March. Iger, who remains on the Disney board, is now a business partner of Josh Kushner — the brother of Trump's son-in-law and diplomatic adviser, Jared Kushner — in striking a deal to buy the NBA's Los Angeles Lakers.

Other outlets are closely watching the growing ABC-FCC confrontation.

CBS' parent company, Paramount, as well as Meta, X and Google, all struck deals similar to the one that ABC reached to resolve lawsuits filed by Trump. The president has also filed private lawsuits against The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times and the BBC over their reporting. The suits are ongoing.

World.title: 'Profits won.' The child safety trial against Meta kicks off in federal court
World.content:
'Profits won.' The child safety trial against Meta kicks off in federal court

toggle caption John Ruwitch/NPR



OAKLAND, Calif. - A landmark trial got underway on Tuesday pitting Meta Platforms against a consortium of states accusing the company of designing its platforms to hook young users and misleading the public about it.

The case is the latest in a web of litigation that aims to hold social media companies accountable for alleged harms to the mental health of young people.

"Meta's business model can be summed up in four simple words: 'hook' the users, 'hold' them for as long as they can, 'harvest' their data, and then 'hide' the truth from the public when making public statements," California Deputy Attorney General Megan O'Neill said in her opening statement on behalf of the states.

Sponsor Message

"It was especially bad for kids," she said.

The stakes in this case are sky-high, with an initial estimate of potential penalties as high as $1.4 trillion — roughly the entire value of Meta's equity on the Nasdaq. Some legal experts compare this moment to landmark litigation against tobacco companies in the 1990s that forced them into big settlements and changed their behavior — and the public discussion about the risks of cigarettes.

Lawyers representing California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey allege that Meta designed its flagship products, Instagram and Facebook, to be addictive to minors with algorithms that "encourage compulsive use" and features like infinite scroll, photo filters and the "like" button. The states say the company knew the platforms were dangerous to kids, but publicly downplayed the risks.

The states also accuse Meta of violating the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA, by gathering personal data about users under 13 and not getting parental consent.

Meta has denied these allegations, and in a statement emailed to NPR, said the states' claims are unsubstantiated, and that the company stands by its record of creating strong protections for teens, including enhanced privacy settings and a one-hour timer on Instagram to remind them to close the app.

Sponsor Message

In court, Paul Schmidt, a lawyer for Meta, argued that the states were cherry picking data points, statements and studies made by Meta out of context, and made the case that Meta was cognizant of the risks to young people and made meaningful efforts to address them.

"Let me be clear: Meta has talked over the years about people struggling with social media," he said in his opening statement to the 8-member advisory jury.

And while Schmidt said there was no dispute that some teens struggle to manage their time on social media apps, or that people can use them to post negative things, "That's something Meta takes seriously, and tries to act on."

"From our perspective, much of this lawsuit is about the government attorneys and their witnesses saying, 'In trying to improve, we'd do it a little differently. In talking about how to improve, we disagree with how you talk about it.' It's meaningful, and the evidence will be meaningful, these efforts Meta has taken to improve," he said.

Social media companies have previously been shielded from some legal actions thanks to both the First Amendment and Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which says they are not accountable for content posted on them by users.

But in this trial, the attorneys are taking a different tack: Instead of holding the company accountable for problematic content, it accuses them of problematic design — specifically, that Facebook and Instagram were designed to keep young users scrolling. The states argue that keeping kids on the site longer boosted Meta's revenue, but harmed kids' mental health.

O'Neill previewed the states' arguments, which rely heavily on internal Meta communications and studies that the states say contradicted many of the company's public statements.

She cited an internal email from 2016 that noted the "overall company goal" for Instagram is "teen time spent" on the platform. She also noted a study entitled "Long Term Retention: The Young Ones Are The Best Ones" that looked into use by tweens, who are approximately 10 to 12 years old, and concluded the earlier a person starts using the platforms, the more likely they are to stay and to generate revenue for the company.

Sponsor Message

At the same time, O'Neill said, Meta's executives were downplaying or denying the addictiveness of the platforms. "Meta said it prioritized safety over profits, but it hid the reality that when it came time to make a decision, time and again profits won," she said.

Meta has already lost two cases in state courts this year over similar claims. In March, a Los Angeles jury found that Meta and Google were to blame for the depression and anxiety of a young woman who compulsively used social media as a small child. They awarded her $6 million in damages.

Separately, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $567 million and implement new safety measures after a jury found that the company failed to protect young users from child sexual exploitation.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the current case has even higher stakes.

"If the current trend continues, they'll lose again, and they'll have to pay a lot again and they'll have to make appropriate changes," Bonta told NPR in an interview before the trial's opening. He said he believes Meta can change its products so that they are not addictive and harmful to children, "and still be wildly successful as a business."

"We want Meta, in short, to stop hurting our kids, stop knowingly hurting our kids, stop using features that you know create mental health harms to kids. I think it's pretty simple," he said. "I think most parents, guardians, teachers know about these harms and want them to stop."

While an initial calculation — submitted by the state attorneys, and later challenged by Meta in pre-trial documents — reveals possible maximum penalties of about $1.4 trillion, Bonta said the states were not seeking a specific amount, and accused Meta of highlighting that number to make the case look unreasonable.

When asked what the figure should be, he did not give an exact number. "They generated revenue of $200 billion last year, so, you know, maybe that amount would be appropriate. Maybe more. Maybe less," he said.

Sponsor Message

Tuesday also saw testimony from the states' first witness, former Meta engineer and whistleblower Arturo Béjar, whom Meta last week attempted to bar from testifying.

Béjar worked at Meta in product safety for eight years over two stints, and testified that he was involved in putting together internal studies that surveyed rates at which users, including youth, reported experiencing harmful content, like bullying, self-harm and violence.

He said that instead of publicizing these results, Meta put out different metrics estimating violations of content policies that did not equate to "harm." "I think that these numbers create a false impression of safety," he said.

In one study of over 200,000 users reporting on encounters with harmful content, he said, "We found that younger people reported higher rates [of harmful encounters] for almost every issue."

Béjar also testified that during his second stint with the company from 2019 to 2021, the company was using the euphemism "problematic use" rather than "addiction."

"'Problematic use' is an example of something where they created a label and it undercounted what in some academic literature is considered to be addiction," he said.

Béjar's testimony will continue on Wednesday.

This trial is being presided over by Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who also presided this spring over the high-profile lawsuit that Tesla CEO Elon Musk brought against OpenAI .

It is expected to last about six weeks, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg may testify, although the attorneys general said Tuesday they had not yet decided whether to call him as a witness.

Legal experts think Meta, which said in late July that an average of 3.6 billion people use its platforms each day, is likely to appeal any ruling against it, potentially up to the Supreme Court.

Note: The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, a charity founded by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, is a financial supporter of NPR.

World.title: S. Korea stresses US alliance amid confusion over Trump drill cut
World.content:
S. Korea stresses US alliance amid confusion over Trump drill cut

toggle caption Yonhap/AP

SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea's president said Tuesday a solid alliance with the United States underpins national security, after U.S. President Donald Trump's abrupt order to "substantially reduce" joint military exercises left many many South Koreans baffled and concerned.

Trump made the surprise announcement in a social media post just before U.S. and South Korean soldiers began Monday's annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which are largely designed to sharpen readiness against North Korean threats.

Trump cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea's refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran.

Sponsor Message

Trump's move was apparently taken without consultations with South Korea and meant to reach out to Kim, deepening concerns about the reliability of the U.S.-South Korean alliance forged in the turmoil of the 1950-53 Korean War.

A weakening of the U.S. defense commitment could shake South Korea's national security as it has no nuclear weapons and is under the U.S. "nuclear umbrella" protection, which guarantees a devastating American response in the event of an attack on its ally by nuclear-armed North Korea. The U.S. has about 28,500 troops in South Korea.

Confidence in the U.S. has already eroded among many South Koreans because of Trump's tariff war and last year's immigration raid in the U.S. state of Georgia that led to the detention of hundreds of South Korean workers.

Trump's announcement "reveals the stark reality of a faltering Korea-U.S. alliance, fueling public anxiety," South Korea's Hankook Ilbo newspaper said in an editorial Tuesday. "It's absurd that the U.S. appears to treat North Korea more respectfully than its ally South Korea."

South Korean leader calls for solid US alliance

In a regular Cabinet meeting, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung stressed the importance of a firm military alliance with the U.S., saying that "national security will be further strengthened when the alliance is solid."

Sponsor Message

"When we build up our strengths, our value and importance as an ally will further grow," said Lee, a liberal who has called for a stronger, self-reliant defense posture.

It was unclear which parts of the 11-day South Korea-U.S. exercises were being downsized. The South Korean and U.S. militaries earlier said their drills this year would be similar in scale to previous years and incorporate lessons from recent conflicts such as North Korea's battlefield experiences on the Russia-Ukraine front. They also said the drills are defensive in nature.

North Korea's Foreign Ministry accused South Korea and the U.S. of plotting more provocative drills this year and vowed to respond with "a new level of a deterrent."

Prospects unclear for reengagement between Trump and Kim

Kim has shunned any talks with the U.S. and South Korea since his earlier high-profile diplomacy with Trump fell apart in 2019.

Experts say Kim won't likely embrace Trump's overture and return to talks anytime soon unless he is promised bigger U.S. concessions. Kim has boosted his military and diplomatic credentials in recent years by enlarging his nuclear arsenal and aligning with Russia over its war against Ukraine.

Lee's presidential office on Monday expressed hopes that a "friendly relationship" between Trump and Kim would lead to "meaningful dialogue" between their countries to promote peace on the Korean Peninsula. That invited a backlash from conservatives, who criticized Lee's government for allegedly prioritizing resumption of Kim-Trump diplomacy over security concerns.

"South Korea's security bulwark is being shaken to its very foundations," Park Chung-kwon, a spokesperson for the main conservative opposition People Power Party, said in a statement.

Doubts about US alliance grow in South Korea

In his social media post, Trump said the military exercises with South Korea are not only costly but "send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea, which he said "has been unthreatening and respectful" during his time in the White House. Trump said he asked Lee if South Korea would join the U.S. in the "denuclearization" of Iran, "and they said, 'No thanks!'"

Sponsor Message

Lee's office said South Korea and the U.S. are closely discussing practical and military contributions that South Korea can make to help restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

"Trump thinks of an alliance as an investment that should pay regular dividends, or a rainy-day fund he can withdraw from when another project isn't going well," said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.

"South Korean leaders understand that relations with the Trump administration will be a constant renegotiation linking economic and security issues. Seoul is thus cautiously responding to recent developments within that framework," Easley said.

World.title: Trump pauses 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods for 3 days
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced late Tuesday he will pause the implementation of 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods for three days, posting the decision less than two hours before the crushing levies were set to take effect.

In an initial online post, the president said he delayed the levies "based on the fact that Canada and the U.S.A., subject to the finalization of documents, have a DEAL!"

A White House declaration later said the suspension is "in the public interest" because Canadian negotiators "expressed a commitment" to concede on trade grievances the Trump administration had cited as the reason for threatening the tariffs in the first place.

In his own statement an hour later, Prime Minister Mark Carney did not speak of a tentative deal and did not say which concessions might have been made. He characterized the administration's decision as a postponement so trade discussions can continue.

"Substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done," read the statement.

"While we continue this work, Canada remains focused on building a stronger, more independent, and more competitive economy at home."

WATCH | Tariffs to be delayed for at least 3 days: Trump pauses 50% tariffs, saying new trade deal reached | Duration 6:27 U.S. President Donald Trump has paused 50 per cent tariffs on Canada, saying the two countries have reached a new trade deal that just needs to be finalized. In a statement, Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'substantial progress has been made.'

The Trump administration's latest round of tariffs were originally scheduled to take effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on Wednesday. The levies would have applied to hundreds of products worth more than $28 billion, from plywood and cement to wine and hockey sticks.

The delay buys time for negotiators who had been racing to reach an agreement ahead of the deadline. It also brings some degree of momentary relief to companies on both sides of the border who worried the fees would devastate small businesses, disrupt supply chains and drive up the cost of living for everyday families.

There is no guarantee Canada can dodge tariffs long-term. Trump did not say whether any deal, if finalized, would lead to the levies' permanent cancellation.

Canadian trade representatives have met with their American counterparts in D.C. a number of times in recent weeks for negotiations Carney previously described as "intense" and "delicate." The prime minister spoke to Trump by phone on Monday and earlier Tuesday.

After the Carney-Trump call, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc again spoke to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to try and close the gap in the negotiating positions.

In a statement after Trump's announcement, Greer said the deal included "comprehensive market access for all American goods, economic security commitments, digital trade alignment, and many important provisions that will continue to protect our market and American workers, along with our Canadian partners," without offering specifics.

Trump suggested a deal could revive Keystone XL, a pipeline project that would have moved oil from Alberta to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries. His online post on Tuesday said the venture, cancelled by the Biden administration in 2021, "may be awoken from the grave!"

Auto tariffs have been a sticking point: sources

Earlier Tuesday, sources cautioned that Canada and the U.S. remained at loggerheads over some finer points, including what sort of tariff, if any, will be applied on Canadian autos bound for the U.S.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the talks.

Trump threatened to hit Canada with the 50 per cent tariffs on a long list of Canadian products ostensibly in retaliation for Ottawa imposing tariffs on some U.S. goods, tariffs that were only levied after Trump launched his trade war on Canada last year.

WATCH | Trade talks expected up until deadline, adviser says: Trade talks with U.S. 'may go down to the wire': Charest | Duration 9:56 With 50 per cent tariffs set to take effect just after midnight, negotiators from Canada and the United States continue to work toward a deal. Member of the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S Economic Relations Jean Charest joins Power & Politics to break down what the state of negotiations means for Canada.

A senior government official previously said Canada was working on a response in the event those tariffs came into effect.

Carney has been weighing a range of options to hit back at the U.S. on trade, including more retaliatory tariffs, the official said. Canada had planned to see the legally binding paperwork on these prospective U.S. tariffs before deciding on an appropriate response.

A key issue in the negotiations has been just how much Canada can get out of the U.S. in exchange for a series of concessions of its own.

LeBlanc has pushed for the U.S. to scrap the new Section 338 tariffs but also lower the existing Section 232 tariffs on industrial products like steel, aluminum, autos and lumber.

WATCH | Entrepreneur says tariffs would ruin his livelihood: Michigan furniture maker says U.S. tariffs threaten his family business | Duration 6:52 Michael Howard, owner of Howard Family Designs, a custom furniture business in Warren, Mich., and says the Trump administration's tariffs on lumber and other goods are driving up costs, making them lose orders and putting his shop's community mentorship program on hold.

The Americans want U.S. liquor back on the shelves of provincially run stores, ending a boycott that has been devastatingly effective. The Trump administration is also pushing for Canada's retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos removed, and tweaks to how the supply-managed dairy sector allocates quotas.

Greer has repeatedly signalled the U.S. is not open to dropping its tariff regime entirely, but there are some signs that the rate may be flexible if the Canadians address some U.S. demands.

Canada wants the U.S. to drive down tariff rates to the lowest possible level, and what's been presented so far by Greer and his team is not satisfactory, sources said.

On autos, the latest U.S. offer would lower the tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles to a headline rate of 15 per cent, down from the current 25 per cent. The headline rate would be the official rate enacted by executive order.

WATCH | NDP on the state of tariff talks: Carney has given 'concession after concession' on U.S. trade: NDP | Duration 0:46 New Democratic Party parliamentary leader Don Davies says Canadians are 'very worried' about the impact new U.S. tariffs could have on Canadian jobs. U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened to hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on a long list of Canadian products if a deal isn't reached by midnight.

But the tariff on Canadian-made vehicles can be reduced further by having more U.S. content, down to an effective rate (the actual duty rate collected) of 7.5 per cent.

Sources said that is still higher than Canada wants.

The new deadline expires at the end of the day on Friday. In the meantime, some Canadian businesses will keep rushing sales out the door to try and beat any levies. Others have already lost American customers because the situation is too volatile.

Bob Rae, a former Canadian ambassador to the United Nations, said Trump's tariffs don't need to take effect to achieve the administration's desired result. The will-they-or-won't-they waiting period creates uncertainty that destabilizes the Canadian economy.

"The whole thing is designed to make Canada feel like a less secure place to do business," Rae told CBC News. "We have to respond in such a way to indicate that, 'No, We're going to continue to go ahead. We're not going to be put off by this.'""

World.title: Who's behind viral online posts fuelling a crisis over migration in Europe?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the days leading up to the largest mass arrival of migrants to Europe in recent years, a short video posted to Instagram garnered 1.4 million views.

It shows a young man submerged up to his neck in water before panning to land in the distance. In the top-right corner, a map traces a sea route from Fnideq, Morocco, to Ceuta, a Spanish enclave on the northern tip of Africa. Responding to comments later, the account holder claimed "we've arrived."

The video was one of many viral posts on Instagram, TikTok and other platforms that appear to have helped mobilize at least two waves of irregular migration from Morocco into Ceuta. The latest, attempted on August 15, led to dozens of arrests.

The accounts belong to several online communities that are part of a broader ecosystem focused on migration-related culture — music, memes and imagery. Some tap into, and appear to be trying to profit from, the desperation of mostly African and Middle Eastern youth seeking better lives abroad.

There is disagreement among governments and organizations over whether a single entity was behind what happened in Ceuta or whether migration was weaponized for geopolitical aims. What is clear is that misinformation, amplified by multiple online communities, helped drive this summer's waves toward Ceuta.

This photo shows a moment from a video which received 1.4 million views on Instagram, was posted just a few days before more than 72,000 people crossed the border from Morocco to Ceuta. (Instagram)

How the crossings took shape online

CBC's visual investigations team, with assistance from Sebastian Vandermeersch of the investigative collective Bellingcat, identified multiple social media accounts, particularly on Instagram, that were active ahead of the first wave on July 30.

The surge in posts was initially triggered by misinformation suggesting a Spanish court ruling meant the country would no longer turn away migrants arriving by sea. Many faceless accounts subsequently began promoting the idea the crossing was possible, using similar language and images. Some posts garnered millions of views.

The consequences were significant: more than 72,000 people crossed the border on July 30, overwhelming authorities in Ceuta and setting off a political crisis in Europe.

The vast majority of those who crossed at the end of July have since returned to Morocco, but at least 5,000 remain in Ceuta, many living on a beach with help from charities. Nearly 100 people died trying to make the crossing.

It is a stark illustration of how misinformation and manipulation can have "real-world impact" when amplified across online communities and directed at people desperate for answers, said Moustafa Ayad, executive director for Africa, the Middle East and Asia at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue. His team has tracked the surge in social media activity over the past month.

A social media post highlights a section of the border fence between Morocco and the Spanish enclave of Ceuta that would be easiest to cross. (Instagram)

Some social media accounts funnelled followers toward WhatsApp chats where users planned crossings and shared information about how to reach Ceuta. Others offered advice directly in their feeds.

One Instagram video titled "the shortest distance," viewed more than 320,000 times, shows a reinforced fence topped with barbed wire and marks the Spanish and Moroccan sides with their respective flags. Large red and yellow arrows — the colours of the Spanish flag — point to a specific section. The message is clear: for someone trying to cross the fence, that is the best spot.

A BBC reporter exchanged direct messages with anonymous accounts that promised advice on entering Ceuta in exchange for money — about $750 in one case — paid up front.

Following the July 30 crossing, Meta and TikTok agreed to fact-check posts in an effort to prevent criminal organizations from using misinformation to exploit would-be migrants for profit.

But another wave of posts began building ahead of August 15, promoted as the next "window" for entering Spain by land and sea. CBC found some of the same accounts that had helped mobilize the July 30 crossing, along with many new accounts created in the days before August 15.

Several posts used variations of the message: "15/08/2026. Everything will become clear on this day."

Reports from Morocco indicate hundreds or more people made their way to the border on August 15.

An Instagram post with a variation on the date and 'Everything will become clear on this day' language. (Instagram)

This time, Moroccan and Spanish authorities were prepared. Thousands of police were deployed on both sides of the border. According to Morocco's state broadcaster, authorities arrested nearly 300 migrants that Saturday.

Ahead of the weekend, the government said it was monitoring "the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin" encouraging the crossing and would act against those responsible.

Several Instagram accounts involved in the July 30 crossing have since been disabled.

Why the messages found an audience

One factor that helped fuel the online surge was that growing numbers of migrants had successfully reached Ceuta even before the Spanish court ruling, according to the Mixed Migration Centre, a migration research organization headquartered in Geneva.

Researchers there found Ceuta, long a destination for migrants, had become the most popular entry point into Spain in the first quarter of this year. According to the International Organization for Migration, the Spanish government reported that more than 2,200 people entered by land by the end of May — three times as many as during the same period a year earlier.

The exact reason is unclear but could include stricter patrols on other migration routes.

Spanish military personnel gather at the border with Morocco in Ceuta, following mass crossings of migrants on foot and by sea from Morocco into Spanish territory, in Ceuta, Spain, August 15, 2026. (Pedro Nunes/Reuters)

"It did play a role in the misinformation that was shaping up on social media, basically presenting a picture like, 'hey, you can make it,'" said Bram Frouws, director of the Mixed Migration Centre.

But Frouws cautioned against attributing the surge itself to social media.

"Social media [and misinformation] didn't shape the desire or the aspiration to migrate," he told CBC from the Netherlands. "The wish to migrate is already there."

Many of the accounts identified by CBC appeared to reflect widespread disillusionment and desperation among young people in North Africa and beyond, using aspirational images and language that valorize migration.

The response to the posts underlines the depth of that desperation.

People waddle through water to enter Spain, and in the background people who just entered Spain return back to Morocco, amid mass crossings of migrants on foot and by sea from Morocco into Spanish territory, in Ceuta, Spain, July 31, 2026. (Jon Nazca/Reuters)

"People are hard up," said Ayad. For young people facing high unemployment — as high as 40 per cent among youth in Morocco, for example — and a lack of political agency or respect for their rights at home, the surge of migration-related messaging is "going to read like 'now is the time.'"

Because Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish enclave in North Africa, provide the only land borders between Africa and a European country, many of the accounts appear to originate in North African countries, including Morocco and Algeria. Other reports suggest some originate in Italy and Turkey.

Some accounts use European or EU flags and mention a number of potential European destinations without explicitly saying they are selling a way to get there.

One account, posting days before the August 15 crossing, showed an image of the Eiffel Tower with the words "Leaving has become our only concern." Another post that day showed a map tracing a swimming route from Fnideq to Ceuta. Another said "and in the end, we will meet in Europe."

That account had changed its username six times, according to its account details. Although it had existed since June 2025, all of its posts were dated August 3.

A post from a social media account shows the Eiffel Tower and the words 'Leaving has become our only concern.' (Instagram)

Every post used a popular Arabic hashtag mentioning Germany, Belgium, Italy, Paris and "al-Ghorba."

The Arabic word "al-Ghorba" has layered meanings encompassing life abroad, exile and alienation from loved ones.

"Immigration isn't running away," says another Instagram account's bio. "It's the search for opportunity."

Influencer-style accounts with similar themes of departure are followed by thousands of people. More than one repeatedly features photos of people in wetsuits posing on beaches or treading water, an apparent reference to the swimming route from Fnideq to Ceuta.

CBC attempted to contact several accounts referencing the July 30 and August 15 waves but received no response.

World.title: Why elaborate (and expensive) dorm room decor reveals have taken over TikTok
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There was a time, back in the olden days us elder millennials called "the early 2000s," when dorm room decor consisted of a "bed in a bag," a milk crate and a shower caddy.

It didn't do much to cheer up the cement room you shared with the Bio major you'd never met until orientation day, but it was something — and it was yours.

Now it would seem, at least according to social media, that the prison cell esthetic is no longer a rite of passage.

"Emily and Hadley, are you ready for your grand reveal?" a professional designer said in a TikTok "dorm reveal" video last week before showing two freshmen their new space — complete with ruffled bedspreads, matching canopied headboards, an accent rug, a sectional sofa, soft lighting, framed art and a vanity.

By Tuesday, it had been viewed 1.5 million times.

Dorm room upgrades — and their reveals — are so popular online that there's a #DormTok hashtag where videos can get millions of views, and Facebook groups like " Dorm Rooms of Mississippi and Beyond" where some 80,000 members swap design ideas.

There are countless magazine articles that list dorm room "essentials" such as dust ruffles and monogrammed pillows, and Pinterest boards full of "cottagecore nature dorm room" and "coastal dream dorm room" inspiration. Even Ikea has a dorm room transformation page on its website, with design suggestions for a "modern whimsy" look that comes with about a $2,700 Cdn price tag.

There are interior designers who specialize in dorm rooms and charge as much as $20,000 US. And, most critically: there are parents willing to foot the bill.

A screen grab of a post on Threads from Aug. 15, 2026, by Bobbie Hall Young. (@bobbie_not_old/Threads)

The U.S. National Retail Federation estimates that college back-to-school shoppers will spend about $14 billion US on dorm and apartment furnishings this season — a 10 per cent jump from last year.

In another video posted this week, a professional designer shows off "all the details" for a dorm room makeover at the University of Mississippi, including floor-length drapes, a carpet runner, a ruffled white couch with throw pillows, side tables, lamps, a coffee table, custom-built padded desk chairs, custom-built headboards, bedside cubbies and matching ottomans to help the girls step into their raised beds.

"Moved the baby of the brood into her dorm at East Tennessee State," posted a mom on Threads earlier this week alongside photos of a similar room makeover: raised beds, matching ottomans, headboards, floral carpeting, and a lit-up makeup vanity on what used to be a desk.

"12 hours to set up but it was worth it," another TikToker writes alongside a video with 3.5 million views where she reveals a carpet, velvet headboard, shelving and floral decor.

A screen grab of an Instagram post by designer Shelly Gates of @MaryMargaretDesigns posted on June 5, 2026. (@MaryMargaretDesigns/Instagram)

What's driving the decor trend?

If you're wondering what-in-the-upholstered-headboard is happening on college campuses these days, you're not alone. The comment sections on the many (and there are many) videos and posts of so-called dorm room reveals flooding social media this month are a mix of admiration, confusion and disbelief.

"Does anyone else think this is insane?" reads a comment on one of the TikTok videos. The comment was liked 30,000 times.

"L iving in a shitty dorm is a part of the college experience," someone commented on another video.

" Remember when we were dropped off wit h a 'bed in a bag' a nd a dream? Take us back," commented another person.

As House Beautiful magazine recently reported, "on-campus living is becoming a full-on design flex," due in part to our influencer culture where curating a certain esthetic has seeped into daily living. And in the U.S. at least, move-in day has become a social media event, reports Today.

The more elaborate dorm transformations being seen online appear to be largely a U.S. trend, and social media is definitely driving their popularity, Trevor Kruse, the CEO of Interior Designers of Canada, told CBC News.

It also doesn't surprise him that student dorm decor is taking off, he added.

"A dorm room is often their first opportunity to create a space of their own that reflects their personalities," Kruse said. "Even small changes to an interior environment can influence mood, productivity, and overall comfort, helping students create a space that supports both learning and downtime."

Mississippi interior designer Shelly Gates, who reportedly charges as much as $20,000 US for a dorm room makeover, says the goal is to make the spaces feel "warm, happy and like home."

"Most dorms start out with cinderblock walls and fluorescent lighting, and honestly, they can feel a little cold and intimidating," Gates told the New York Post last week.

WATCH | People keep hurting themselves in these Zara pants: Why these trendy Zara pants are called 'death trousers’ | Duration 1:20 I'm sure many of us enjoy a stylish pair of pants — but not if they cause injuries. That's apparently what's happening to people wearing one of Zara's trending trousers. CBC's Puneet Nijjar explains what the heck is going on.

Is it happening here?

Decorating your own space isn't new. But while professional-grade overhauls appear to be mostly in the U.S. — and especially the southern states — there are signs a more subdued version of the trend could be creeping north.

On Pinterest Canada, for instance, dorm-related searches are trending, while "dorm room" searches on Google Trends are up 40 per cent compared to this time last year. On Facebook, there's a "University Dorm Room Moms - Canada" group with 13,000 members posting practical questions about under-bed storage space, mattress toppers and duvets.

And Canadian retailer Simons has a dorm decor section on its website, advertising "w himsical objects, bold patterns and contrasting colours to create a room" with personality.

Kruse notes that while Canadian students certainly personalize their dorm rooms, Canadian schools may have restrictions about how much can be changed.

Audrey Leveridge, 17, says she found some inspiration on Pinterest for her upcoming move into residence at Queen's University in Kingston, Ont., and bought some decor based on her preferred colour palette.

"I think lots of people are planning on doing dorm decorations with themes, though," she told CBC News.

"I haven't heard of any overhauls but I know people like to make it look as nice as possible, more homey and their own."

World.title: Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo: What's going on and why is the outbreak so alarming?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is officially the deadliest in the country’s history, and health officials worry the crisis will only get worse when children return to school.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo became the deadliest in the country’s history this week as confirmed cases continue to rise at a pace that is raising alarm around the world.

At least 2,378 deaths have been recorded in the D.R.C. as of Aug. 16, the country’s public health ministry said in its latest update on Tuesday.

"This is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, and it is moving faster than any previous Ebola outbreak. That's why I call it unprecedented speed," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, head of the World Health Organization (WHO), said on Tuesday.

"We must be frank: the epidemic is far from being under control. It had a big head start, and we are still playing catch-up."

Here's what you need to know about Ebola and the current outbreak.

WATCH | WHO says Ebola spreading at 'unprecedented' rate: Ebola outbreak in Congo deemed fastest-spreading on record | Duration 2:37 The Democratic Republic of Congo has now recorded over 2,000 deaths in what the World Health Organization is calling the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record.

What is Ebola?

Ebola is a serious disease linked to what's known as orthoebolaviruses.

There are different strains of orthoebolaviruses, including four that affect humans: Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo. The Bundibugyo strain has been identified in the current outbreak, the D.R.C.'s 17th on record.

Humans can contract Ebola through close contact with the blood or bodily fluids of infected animals such as fruit bats or chimpanzees. It then passes between people when contact is made with the bodily fluids of someone who is sick or has died from Ebola, or with contaminated objects.

When and where did the current outbreak begin?

Formally declared in May, the outbreak has centred on the eastern D.R.C., near the border with South Sudan and Uganda. Uganda also identified cases but declared itself "Ebola free" in late July.

According to the WHO, the first suspected case was a health worker who had reported symptoms on April 24 and later died at a medical centre in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province.

Health workers disinfect a wooden coffin before loading the body of an unidentified man, who according to his family died of Ebola, as they retrieve it from his house in Bunia, Ituri province, D.R.C., on July 10. (Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters)

Why is this outbreak so concerning?

The speed at which Ebola is spreading this time far eclipses previous outbreaks.

For example, 100 days after the first Ebola case was confirmed in the D.R.C. in 2018, 323 cases were reported, according to data cited by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Similarly, 398 cases were reported in Guinea at the 100-day mark in 2014.

In the current outbreak, which has yet to reach the 100-day mark, 5,021 cases were reported in the D.R.C. as of Aug. 16, according to the country's public health ministry.

Cases have been confirmed in six D.R.C. provinces, but the vast majority of cases and deaths have been in Ituri. The ministry says the outbreak also has a case fatality rate of 47.4 per cent, and the United Nation's humanitarian aid chief Tom Fletcher said last week that a person is dying every 30 minutes.

What factors are complicating the response?

The first is that there currently is no vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola. (Two vaccine trials, including one in Canada, have begun, but it will likely take months before a wide-scale rollout.)

Armed conflict and mass internal displacement in the eastern D.R.C., regular movement between countries in the border areas and a lack of resources also are important factors. At the same time, residents have been distrustful of the government and public health efforts.

"People who are getting sick are not actively presenting themselves to doctors, hospitals, health-care workers … because they're scared," said Dr. Tyler Evans, a U.S.-based public health physician who has worked on past Ebola outbreaks. "They see Ebola treatment units, these white tents — they're seeing half of these people go in, and they're not coming out.

"All of those [factors] together is really contributing to this perfect storm."

WATCH | How long will it take to contain the outbreak?: It’ll take at least 6 months to contain Ebola outbreak in Congo: experts | Duration 1:38 There are 4,400 known cases of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Officials say there are far more cases that haven’t been recorded. While trials for a vaccine are underway, it’s not ready yet — and as Congo is a central country in Africa, there are concerns the outbreak could spread beyond its borders.

What can — and needs to — be done?

Testing and contact tracing are key, said Dr. Joanne Liu, a physician and professor at McGill University in Montreal who was involved in the response to an Ebola outbreak in West Africa from 2014 to 2016.

That, coupled with safe funerals and treatment in isolation, can help get a "fuller picture" of where the outbreak is going, Liu told CBC. She also said more health workers need to be deployed and protected as they do their work.

A WHO official told reporters from Bunia in Ituri province on Tuesday that the agency is scaling up its response and engaging local communities. Dr. Thierno Baldé, the WHO's incident manager for the disease in the D.R.C., said 100 additional epidemiologists will be deployed while more than 400 beds have been added over the past two weeks.

Liu said Canada and other countries that are concerned about the spread of Ebola should provide more financial support to help teams on the ground.

"If you want to not have a wildfire coming to you, you need to control it where it's happening — not barricading yourself and then closing your border," Liu said. "That might have a small effect, but that will not do the trick in getting control over the outbreak."

World.title: New research discovers the twisty secret behind the narwhal's unusually straight tusk
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The narwhal tusk is a true oddity in the natural world.

Reaching up to three metres in length, the tusk is an upper tooth that grows through the whale's lip on the left side. And it is the only mammal tusk that grows perfectly straight, with no curves.

A team of international researchers believe they have figured out why it grows so straight — and the answer lies in its unique pattern of opposing spirals.

“This was really the first time that we could prove that this was the case and that there were two opposing spirals … that was really quite surprising to us,” said study author Henrik Birkedal from Aarhus University in Denmark.

Opposing spirals

New research published in the journal Nature Communications breaks down how the two opposing spirals — one going right, the other going left — allow the tusk to grow straight.

The project began when Birkedal was approached by an organic chemistry colleague who was looking at why some molecules are right-handed and some left-handed.

The colleague had been visiting Greenland and heard that narwhal tusk spirals all go in the same direction, to the left. Birkedal decided to look into it.

Birkedal’s team collaborated with biologists from Greenland and physicists from Sweden to better understand the molecular structure of the tusks and spirals.

“We really set out to try and understand how the spiralling tusk is related to the underlying structure of the tusk,” he said.

This closeup of a narwhal's head shows the tusk protruding from its mouth, as well as the distinctive spirals on the outside. (Mads Peter Heide-Jørgensen)

And what they found wasn’t just a simple spiral.

The tusks, which are mostly found on male narwhals, are made of dentine and cementum, similar to human teeth but without the hard layer of enamel.

Through advanced imaging techniques that Birkedal described as being similar to CT scans, the researchers found two opposing spirals — a left-handed spiral on the outer layer of cementum, and a right-handed one in the inner layer of dentine.

It's an important discovery, not just in solving the mystery of the narwhal's straight tusk but for its potential to help shed light on the structural principles of human bones on other similar instances, Birkedal said.

A sensory organ

Martin Nweeia, a narwhal biologist and specialist in marine mammal teeth at Harvard University, said he was delighted to see the research's deep-dive into what he calls "the most extraordinary tooth on the planet."

“Naturally, when a curious dentist meets the most extraordinary tooth, there's an irresistible urge to figure out what's going on here,” he told CBC News.

However, Nweeia — who was not associated with this study — said he was surprised to see the researchers characterize the tusk’s function as “speculative” in the initial pages of the paper.

Martin Nweeia is narwhal biologist and specialist in marine mammal teeth at Harvard University. He said his research has found that the tusk's main function is primarily as a sensory organ. (Paul Nicklen)

“I'm not sure where they got this,” he said.

Nweeia contends that teeth are multifunctional. But in the case of the narwhal, his research has shown the tusk's main function is primarily as a sensory organ, rather than being used for defence or for feeding.

“Do we use our teeth for self-defence? No. But if someone grabbed us around the neck, might we bite them? Sure,” he said.

That said, Nweeia commended the study authors for devoting the energy and effort to learning more about narwhals, and says he is always cheering on anyone who tries to discover more about them.

Future research

When looking ahead to future research projects about narwhals, Nweeia said he hopes to see more off-season studies and collaboration with Indigenous communities.

The Canadian Arctic is home to most of these mammals in the summer. The off-season, he said, is when Inuit knowledge becomes critical because scientists typically only go up for a month or two when there’s more availability to study the animals, while they are not under the sea ice cover.

“To have that link that ties everything together, you take science, you take traditional knowledge, and you take the value that the Inuit observations have,” said Nweeia.

He was a part of a study in 2024 that showed the capability of narwhal tusks to bend and flex 12 degrees in every direction.

Narwhals during spring migration make their way to Baffin Island in northern Canada. There are few opportunities to study the whales, which live under sea ice for more than half the year. (Glenn Williams)

“If you've ever seen a narwhal tusk, you would never imagine that thing could bend and be flexible,” said Nweeia.

He didn’t think it was possible when he first heard about it through interviews with Inuit elders. Yet through science and study, they found it to be true.

“These are the components I think that really make a study what I call integrative — that you take different fields of science and that you look at something from multiple perspectives.”

Birkedal agrees that interdisciplinary work is crucial. His recent paper was only possible because of the involvement of teams in Greenland and Sweden.

“It's also a good example of how when disciplines meet, you can really learn from each other to do something that you wouldn't be able to do on your own," he said.

World.title: Will the PQ's Trump-era referendum pause work with voters?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A referendum is coming — just not now.

That was the message from Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon during a round of media interviews on Tuesday.

Just over a week before the start of Quebec’s election campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon released a statement early in the day saying he would not hold a sovereignty referendum while U.S. President Donald Trump remains in office.

Trump’s term ends on Jan. 20, 2029.

That would leave St-Pierre Plamondon over a year and a half to hold a referendum before the end of his first mandate — assuming his party wins a majority in Quebec’s Oct. 5 election.

In an interview with CBC News, St-Pierre Plamondon said he is clarifying his party's intentions ahead of the election campaign. The next government will be focused on "reversing problems" caused by the reigning Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ).

"It's not a pushback. We've been saying there would be a referendum within the first four years," he said. "Now we are being more precise."

He said the situation with the U.S. has been influencing Canadian politics, starting with Mark Carney's "elbows up" campaign — using fear to erase Justin Trudeau's tenure from voters' memories, he said.

An attempt to 'defuse the issue,' pollster says

St-Pierre Plamondon’s announcement comes amid economic anxiety surrounding impending U.S. tariffs. The last round of tariffs was a major blow to the Quebec economy.

Philippe Fournier, a poll analyst, said much remains unclear ahead of the start of the provincial campaign, with the PQ holding a small lead over the Quebec Liberal Party in opinion polls.

But one thing is clear: most voters don’t want another referendum, at least not now.

“It was the best possible strategy to try to appease voters who are concerned about the uncertainty caused by the Trump administration, the tariffs, and just the global uncertainty,” Fournier said of the PQ leader’s announcement.

“This is an attempt by Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon to defuse this issue. I’m not sure it will work.”

Opposition parties were quick to pounce on St-Pierre Plamondon’s move.

PQ leader slammed as 'referendum weather vane'

Éric Duhaime, leader of the Conservative Party of Quebec, which is opposed to another referendum, labelled St-Pierre Plamondon a “referendum weather vane.”

“How can anyone trust someone who spent five years repeating that he would achieve independence at all costs, and then changes his mind one week before the election? If another protectionist government takes power in Washington, what will he do? Postpone his project yet again?” Duhaime said.

“Quebec does not have to have its political agenda dictated by the Americans.”

Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard said the postponement indicates “separating Quebec from Canada is a weak option” and that the PQ isn’t being clear about its intentions.

“It’s a party that’s saying yes and no at the same time,” Milliard said.

Christine Fréchette, Quebec's current premier and the leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec, said the announcement was “irresponsible” given the looming tariffs.

The PQ has been in power multiple times since the last, near-miss referendum in 1995, but has avoided putting the question to voters for a third time.

St-Pierre Plamondon, however, maintains a PQ government would hold a referendum within its first mandate.

He said nobody is disappointed with the timeline now that it is more precise. Now his party intends to a run a campaign that is "clear and solid on every topic."

Fournier said St-Pierre Plamondon’s plan could appeal to “soft nationalist voters who may not be keen on a referendum but want to see Fréchette replaced.”

He added: “The question is, will it work? I’m not sure about that.”

World.title: Remains of 3rd missing person found at same property near Ottawa
World.content:
Provincial police say they have found a third set of human remains at a property near Smiths Falls in eastern Ontario. They have identified the latest remains as Lawrence Bertrim, who was last seen in 2022.

Provincial police say they have found a third set of human remains at a property near Smiths Falls in eastern Ontario.

They have identified the latest remains as those of Lawrence Bertrim, who was last seen in downtown Smiths Falls in September 2022.

Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) said they're still determining the cause of his death, and no charges have been laid. A $50,000 reward for information leading to a conviction in his case remains on offer, police said.

Bertrim was 42 at the time of his disappearance.

"Locating Lawrence Bertrim is a significant development for his family, who have waited nearly four years for answers, and for the investigative team, who have worked relentlessly on this case," said OPP Det. Insp. Jennifer Patton in the news release.

"We understand the public interest generated by the discovery of three missing persons on a single property, and we ask for patience as investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads."

Police said Bertrim's remains were found on the Kelly Jordan Road property on Aug. 6, the day after they announced they had found the body of another missing man, Robert Lambert, on the same property in July.

No charges have been laid in Lambert's death, but police said at the time they suspected foul play.

The remains of Robbie Thomson were found on the same residential property in October 2025. Four people have been charged in connection with his death, including three suspects charged with first-degree murder.

Bertrim and Thomson knew each other, according to reporting by CBC News in 2023. At the time, the pair were believed to have also known 34-year-old Steven Tate, whose body was discovered in a ditch along Highway 15 in November 2023.

Tate's death and the disappearance of Bertrim and Thomson gripped the Smiths Falls area, and the discoveries of the first two sets of remains deeply affected the small town and surrounding rural area, according to the local reeve.

World.title: Drunk driver who killed 2 in 2024 crash pre-approved for day parole
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A woman who drove the wrong way down a divided highway and collided with another vehicle, killing the two people inside, has been pre-approved for day parole when she is eligible for it next month.

Brittany Barry, 35, pleaded guilty to drunk driving causing the deaths of Laura Hannah, 53, and Jamie Hannah, 20, and injuring her own two children, who were in the vehicle with her.

The crash happened on Oct. 19, 2024, on Highway 11 near Dundurn, about 35 kilometres southeast of Saskatoon.

Barry is about a year and a half into serving her six-year prison sentence, which was imposed on March 14, 2025.

Federal prisoners are eligible for full parole after serving one-third of their sentence, and can apply for day parole six months before that.

In a decision dated Aug. 11, the Parole Board of Canada approved Barry's application to be released to a community-based residential facility, commonly known as a halfway house, when she is eligible for day parole.

Family members outside of Saskatoon provincial court in March 2025 hold a picture of Laura and Jamie Hannah, who were killed when Brittany Barry's truck collided with their vehicle. (Liam O'Connor/CBC)

The parole board noted that family members of the victims "feel that it is too soon for you to be released to the community and that you should be disentitled to any form of absences or conditional release based upon the severity of your crime."

The board said it also considered Barry's acceptance of responsibility and the work she has done on personal growth.

"To honour the victims, you said that you intend to live a life of sobriety and never again let yourself get to that point in your life where you return to criminal behaviours," the parole board wrote.

"You believe that you can honour your children by being there for them as a mother and making better decisions that do not place them at risk."

The board said that Barry has remained in minimum security while serving her sentence, and there have not been any concerns regarding her behaviour.

The board's decision also authorized "leave privileges" while Barry is at the halfway house. Her plan includes unescorted temporary absences to visit her family, attend church and attend Alcoholics Anonymous meetings.

The board imposed several conditions on Barry's day parole, including that she is prohibited from consuming alcohol, must not go into any bars, must not drive, and must continue to take treatment and counselling as directed.

She is also to have "no direct or indirect contact" with the family of the victims, with the exception of her own children.

The decision acknowledged that Barry is already subject to a seven-year driving prohibition as part of her sentence, but said the no-driving condition would help "reinforce this."

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.
