I doubt that restrictive clothing, against the backdrop of the stress of adapting to school, will help a child develop a sense of belonging to school life,” says Ilia’s mother, Taya Maharashvili.

Taya plans to contact the Education Ministry and demand stronger justification for making school uniforms compulsory:

“I have never opposed introducing a dress code. I believe it is important to dress appropriately in educational and professional environments, and children should learn this from an early age. However, the uniform proposed by the ministry is unacceptable.”

Introducing school uniforms for pupils in the lower grades of public schools is one element of a planned large-scale education reform. Education Minister Givi Mikanadze announced the measure on 2 December 2025 during a presentation of the National Concept for General Education Reform.

“School uniforms will help create an environment focused on learning and foster a sense of belonging to the educational institution. They will also reduce visible differences in pupils’ socio-economic backgrounds,” Mikanadze said.

School uniforms were compulsory in Georgia in the past. In Soviet schools, pupils wore dark brown, black or blue uniforms with white aprons. In independent Georgia, only some private schools require uniforms, although parents there have also complained about the quality of the fabric.

Polyester, viscose and elastane — what materials are used to make the clothes?

School uniform design. Photo: Education Ministry

The appearance, colour and quality of the school uniforms were determined entirely by the state. The boys’ uniforms will be plain dark blue, while the girls’ uniforms will feature a checked pattern. The state emblem will appear on the left side of the jacket.

The uniforms are made mainly from synthetic materials: 72% polyester, 25% viscose and 3% elastane.

The jackets will also have polyester lining. According to ministry documents, only the skirts will have cotton lining.

The uniforms can be washed at 40°C and ironed at 110°C. Bleach is prohibited, as is ironing the emblem or dry-cleaning the garment.

The school uniform set will include a jacket and trousers for boys, and a jacket and skirt (or a jacket and trousers) for girls.

“First of all, this uniform is uncomfortable. It reminds me of a situation where a paediatric dietitian insists that a child eat vegetables, only for the child to spit them out. I have the feeling that the ministry employs people who have no idea what children and childhood are like,” Taya says.

One uniform set will cost 95 lari. Some pupils will receive it for free.

Trousers and skirts will cost 25 lari, while a jacket will cost 45 lari. A set may include a jacket and two pairs of trousers, or a jacket, trousers and a skirt. As a result, one school uniform will cost parents 95 lari.

Most parents say one set will not be enough for a child to wear throughout the week. Pupils will also need a white shirt or T-shirt under the uniform, which parents will have to buy separately.

Pupils from socially vulnerable families will receive uniforms free of charge. This applies to families registered in the Unified Database of Socially Vulnerable Persons with a rating score below 65,001.

Children in state care or foster families, as well as those living in family-type homes or shelters for children without parental care, will also receive uniforms free of charge.

Ukrainian pupils who have been living and studying in Georgia since the start of the war will also receive school uniforms free of charge.

Is the uniform fabric safe? What should parents do if their child has an allergy or skin condition?

Third-grader Sandro has urticaria and allergic dermatitis. That is why his mother, Sopho, who is raising him alone, pays close attention to the quality of his clothes.

“My son is at school from 9:30am until 6pm, and I am concerned about everything: the quality, comfort and presence of allergens,” says Sopho Trapaidze.

Polyester, the material used for the uniforms, is widely used in the textile industry because it is durable and inexpensive. However, doctor Eka Kvirkvelia notes that the material is not suitable for everyone and is not hypoallergenic for all people. In some cases, it can contribute to overheating, increased sweating and skin irritation.

“True hypoallergenicity depends not only on the composition, but also on the fabric’s breathability, the chemical composition of dyes, production standards and the lining material. It is also important to understand that ‘international practice’ does not mean there is a single standard: different countries use different approaches. Nevertheless, natural fabrics or materials with a high cotton content are often preferred for primary school pupils,” she wrote on social media.

According to her, assessing the quality of school uniforms should rely on specific indicators, such as the percentage of each component, dermatological test results and data on children’s safety, rather than broad claims such as “hypoallergenic”.

Taya Maharashvili has also begun looking at practices in other countries. Polyester is used in schools in some developed countries, but there is one important detail:

“The percentage of polyester in our school uniforms is higher than in those countries. In addition, such countries more often introduce a dress code rather than a uniform. How the fabric has been treated and whether it meets safety standards are also important. They say these factors were taken into account when the Georgian school uniform was designed. However, the public should demand more reliable information supported by evidence, such as expert assessments and so on.”

Education Ministry says exceptions will be allowed

Parents are already demanding additional evidence from the Education Ministry that the fabric meets safety and quality standards. They are also calling on doctors to help address the issue.

“We demand a change in the fabric used for school uniforms. Synthetic clothing is harmful to children’s health,” Tamuna Gagnidze writes.

Dozens of parents have left comments under her post making similar demands. Many say they do not intend to dress their children in the uniforms.

“My child cannot wear polyester: he has atopic dermatitis, and contact with this material makes his skin worse. I absolutely do not want the school uniform to cause bleeding wounds on his skin,” says Hatuna Laghadze in a comment.

Sopho Trapaidze also does not plan to buy a new uniform for her son Sandro. She plans to make it herself — in the same style and colour, but from higher-quality material.

The Education Ministry says it will take into account cases where pupils have officially confirmed medical contraindications.

The Georgian Law on General Education regulates such cases. Article 19¹, paragraph 3, states that “a primary school pupil may be exempted from the obligation to wear a school uniform on health grounds based on a written agreement with the Ministry of Education”.

The ministry says such cases will be considered individually. Parents will need to provide the school with the relevant medical certificate. The pupil will still have to follow the established dress code.

What happens if a parent does not put their child in a school uniform?

School uniforms are compulsory. The ministry has placed particular emphasis on this point.

“Will they (officials — JAMnews) dress their own children in clothes made from this fabric?” This is the most common question in school groups and social media discussions about the uniforms.

“What happens if I do not put this uniform on my child? Will they be banned from going to school?” one parent asks in the comments.

“I have three school-age children. I am not going to buy it either. I consulted lawyers, and no one has the right to create problems for children because of this,” another parent replies.

When presenting the new uniforms, Education Minister Givi Mikanadze said that if parents refuse to use them, the school may address the issue through educational and disciplinary measures. The law does not specify which sanctions schools can impose.

The ministry says schools will consider each refusal on an individual basis. Each school will be able to find its own solution based on its internal rules.

What is known about the Chinese company making Georgia’s school uniforms?

School uniform production process. Photo: Educational Resources LLC

All matters related to the logistics of the school uniforms are handled by Educational Resources LLC, a department established within the Education Ministry in March 2026.

The ministry initially planned to manufacture the uniforms in Georgia. It considered using sewing workshops at state vocational colleges.

On 3 April 2026, the ministry announced a market study to procure the school uniforms. On 29 April, Educational Resources requested government approval to use a simplified procurement procedure. However, on 14 May, it emerged that the company initially selected did not meet the ministry’s requirements. The ministry had to restart the market study.

In June, the ministry signed a contract with Glory Textile Industry LLC to supply the school uniforms through direct negotiations, without a tender. The Education Ministry opted for direct negotiations to save time, as it needed to secure the uniforms and have them delivered before the start of the new school year.

Glory Textile Industry was registered in Georgia on 10 March 2026. Its sole owner and director is Chinese citizen Liu Xiaolin. The company received the order to manufacture the school uniforms just two months after its establishment and signed a 45.66 million lari contract with the Georgian government.

The company must deliver 1,801,000 items of clothing to Georgia between 25 August and 30 November:

Girls’ jackets — 292,000;

Boys’ jackets — 308,000;

Girls’ trousers — 438,000;

Boys’ trousers — 616,000;

Skirts — 146,000;

Long skirts — 1,000.

The uniforms are being made in China’s Jiangsu province at the Eton Kidd factory, which is operated by the SUMEC group.

Eton Kidd is a major Chinese school uniform brand. According to its official website, the company was founded in 2009. It works with more than 3,400 schools across 31 provincial-level administrative divisions, manufacturing and supplying school uniforms.

According to official information, SUMEC is an important subsidiary of the China National Machinery Industry Corporation (SINOMACH) and belongs to a group of state-owned enterprises directly under the central government of China.

Glory Textile Industry plans to deliver the school uniforms to Georgia in three stages:

Stage I — 301,000 items — by 25 August 2026;

Stage II — 600,000 items — by 15 October 2026;

Stage III — 900,000 items — by 30 November 2026.

First batch of uniforms arrives in Georgia. Where can parents get them?

The first batch of school uniforms has already arrived in Georgia. According to Educational Resources, the quantity is sufficient for first-graders.

The uniforms are currently being sorted into sets. Sales will begin on 1 September and continue until 14 September.

First batch of school uniforms. Photo: Educational Resources LLC

In the coming days, the uniforms will be distributed to major cities and regions. The authorities will also announce where parents can buy them. Parents will pay for the uniforms by cashless payment.

Uniforms for pupils in grades 2-6 will arrive later and will be distributed in two stages, on 15 October and 30 November.

This means pupils in grades 2-6 will not have uniforms in September. At the start of the school year, parents will have to buy regular clothes and purchase the uniforms later.

Will school uniforms change anything in Georgia’s education system?

The government is spending 45.66 million lari on school uniforms, saying they will help reduce social inequality. Meanwhile, Georgian schools still do not provide free meals.

According to a 2023 study by Georgia’s National Statistics Office, with support from UNICEF, only 27% of children aged 6 to 17 eat at school every day. Meanwhile, 34.9% do not eat at all during the school day. Among children from low-income families, the figure reaches 44.9%.

The same study found that 83.2% of parents believe schools should provide children with meals during the school day. In some Georgian schools, particularly in the regions, children cannot even buy food because the schools have no canteens.

Against the backdrop of these and other problems, school uniforms appear to be the least pressing issue facing Georgia’s public schools.

“I cannot support spending such a large amount of money on uniforms when schools have yet to address basic problems with toilets, canteens and the quality of education,” says Ana Gvaladze.

“We called the ministry 80 times to get the problem with the toilets at School No. 161 resolved,” adds Sopho Trapaidze.

Taya, who has been studying education issues in depth, says building a school culture is a complex process and involves much more than a set of behavioural rules:

“Schools face many problems today, from poor infrastructure and failures to meet health and hygiene standards to a lack of an emotionally safe environment for children. Children attend dull, grey schools. Sometimes a school has just one teacher, who provides the support that the education system as a whole should provide. So school culture cannot be strengthened through uniforms alone. Likewise, in such an unhealthy environment — and given the problems with crime in the country — uniforms cannot stop bullying.”

Taya notes that bullying does not actually start because of clothing.

“Clothing is just an excuse. If a bully is looking for a victim, they can pick on someone’s height, weight, glasses, shoes, bag or even pen. Uniforms cannot hide social differences. And most importantly, when the minister talked about school culture and a sense of belonging, did he forget that a child who is hungry because their school has no canteen will not develop any sense of belonging?”

Hundreds of thousands of Georgian schoolchildren will start the new academic year in “impoverished” conditions, in buildings that are not suitable for proper education. In recent years, hundreds of schools across the country have been demolished, while construction on many replacements has yet to begin.

School uniforms in Georgia

World.title: Former Georgian PM Irakli Garibashvili accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail
World.content:
Former PM accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail

Jailed former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has accused Georgian Dream honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili and the current government of blackmail.

In a statement released from prison on 17 August 2026, the former prime minister claimed he was being pressured to plead guilty to new corruption charges and permanently withdraw from politics at Ivanishvili’s demand. It is the first time that a former close ally of Ivanishvili has openly spoken out against the founder of the ruling party.

Plea deal ultimatum and plan to quit politics

A photograph of a printed letter dated 17 August was posted on the Facebook pages of Garibashvili and his wife, Nunuka Tamazashvili. Only four paragraphs of the letter were made public. It is unclear who wrote the letter or how it was delivered.

According to the published document, the government is offering the former prime minister a compromise. Under the proposed terms, Garibashvili would have to plead guilty to a new corruption-related charge.

The letter sets out the proposal in detail:

“They are offering me the option of pleading guilty in one case, where everything would be arranged by agreement, including a confession, witness signatures and so on. They are offering a plea bargain while retaining the same five-year sentence: that is, as it has been explained to me, the sentences would be combined, but the final term would remain five years.”

According to the document, a corruption conviction would serve as a form of “insurance” for the government, aimed at preventing the former prime minister from returning to politics in the future.

Two options and a political condition

The published letter refers to investigations into several cases. Its author suggests that these could result in corruption charges.

The text outlines two possible courses of action for Garibashvili. The first would involve continuing to contest the case in court.

“Let’s discuss this seriously and see it through to the end,” the document says.

The second option is presented as a compromise. According to the letter, Garibashvili would plead guilty in one of the cases, with the details agreed in advance:

“Let’s plead guilty in one case, where everything will be arranged by agreement: a confession, witness signatures and so on.”

The document also says that a new plea deal would not increase the five-year prison sentence already imposed on Garibashvili. The sentences would be combined, leaving the overall term unchanged at five years.

However, the proposal comes with a political condition.

“After leaving, you cannot engage in politics. If it is decided to ‘renege on the agreements’, then the corruption charges that will be brought will serve as an insurance mechanism, preventing even the thought of returning to politics,” the document says.

The authenticity of the letter has not been independently verified, and its author remains unknown. There is also no confirmation that new cases are in fact being prepared against Garibashvili.

Garibashvili’s first open confrontation with Ivanishvili

This marks Irakli Garibashvili’s first public confrontation with Bidzina Ivanishvili. For many years, Garibashvili was regarded as one of his most loyal political allies.

He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister, first from 2013 to 2015 and again from 2021 to 2024.

Garibashvili was sentenced under a plea agreement reached on 12 January 2026. He was given a five-year prison term and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated from him.

The case concerned the laundering of illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. Garibashvili is currently serving his sentence in a prison in Rustavi.

The new statement means that the former prime minister himself is now linking possible further legal action against him to demands that he stay out of politics. However, the material made public so far presents only Garibashvili’s version of events.

Response from MP Irma Inashvili, named in letter

The letter published by Garibashvili mentions MP Irma Inashvili and Dito Chubinidze. According to the text, they — along with “supporters like them” and campaigns on social media — have raised suspicions.

“Supporters such as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili, as well as campaigns organised on social media, have raised very serious suspicions and caused us tangible harm,” the document says.

Inashvili denied any involvement in organised campaigns. She said Irakli Garibashvili was her friend, but that she expressed her views publicly and independently.

“I have never planned or conducted any campaigns on social media; I don’t need such campaigns — I already express my views openly in my own name!” Inashvili wrote.

She said Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze was the main target of her criticism.

“I expose Kobakhidze and fight against him,” Inashvili said.

Opposition says Garibashvili being politically neutralised

Opposition figures have described Garibashvili’s letter as a sign of an internal conflict within the government. Their comments amount to political assessments and do not independently corroborate the circumstances described in the letter.

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said the contents of the letter pointed to a political motive behind Garibashvili’s imprisonment.

“Ivanishvili’s bargaining with Garibashvili — ‘I will punish you even more severely unless you give me guarantees that you will leave politics for good’ — confirms that the motive for his arrest is neither to punish a corrupt official nor to fight corruption in general, nor does it serve any public or state interest. It serves Bidzina’s personal political interests,” Gvaramia wrote.

He also qualified his comments by noting that the authenticity of the letter had not been established. Gvaramia particularly highlighted what he described as an attempt to politically neutralise Garibashvili.

Levan Samushia, a member of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, linked the statement to the country’s current system of governance. He said any potential threat against Garibashvili’s family warranted a legal response.

“It is clear that Garibashvili is speaking about a possible, alleged threat to his family. This is an issue that requires particular attention and, naturally, provides grounds for launching an investigation,” Samushia said.

Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, said he preferred to wait for further information before reaching a definitive conclusion. Nevertheless, he linked the developments to an internal conflict within Georgian Dream.

“The situation appears alarming because it concerns his family, and at this point clarity is the best means of protecting him and his loved ones,” Sichinava said.

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, described Garibashvili’s case as a warning to current government figures.

“Garibashvili’s case should be learnt by heart by Ivanishvili’s current servants, officials and representatives of the financial sector who justify the government,” Dekanoidze wrote.

Government silent as questions remain unanswered

At the time of writing, reports about Garibashvili’s allegations had not appeared on the websites or Facebook pages of the pro-government Imedi and Rustavi 2 television channels.

Government representatives have yet to respond publicly to the central allegation. They have not said whether Bidzina Ivanishvili had any involvement in sending the letter to Garibashvili. It also remains unclear whether any new investigations into the former prime minister are under way.

Background: From alliance to prison

For many years, Irakli Garibashvili was regarded as one of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s closest political allies. He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister.

On 24 October 2025, Garibashvili was charged with laundering illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. A plea agreement was reached on 12 January 2026, under which the former prime minister was sentenced to five years in prison and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated. He has since been serving his sentence at a penitentiary facility in Rustavi.

Legal proceedings against former senior figures in the ruling team were preceded by internal party disagreements and arrests of officials from various state agencies. There have also been reports of investigative measures involving members of Garibashvili’s family.

The developments suggest that the power struggle within Georgian Dream has entered an increasingly acute phase.

World.title: Uzbekistan steps up tourism cooperation with Russia through new deal
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 19. Uzbekistan’s Tourism Committee and the Federation of Independent Trade Unions of Russia have signed an agreement to expand tourism cooperation, including through special travel programs for Russian trade union members and their families.

This was reflected in the statement by the National Committee of Tourism of Uzbekistan, following a meeting between Committee Deputy Chairman S. Tajiyev and a delegation from the Federation of Independent Trade Unions of Russia.

According to the committee, the sides also discussed prospects for increasing tourist exchanges and developing joint initiatives.

''The meeting highlighted the potential of Russian trade unions, which represent workers at major enterprises and organizations, to help generate organized tourist flows to Uzbekistan,'' the National Committee of Tourism says.

The sides proposed jointly developing several tourism segments, including family and children's tourism, health and wellness tourism, medical tourism, cultural and educational tourism, ecotourism and ski tourism. Special travel programs could be created for trade union members and their families.

Particular attention was given to pilgrimage tourism, especially for residents of Russia's Tatarstan, Bashkortostan and other regions. Potential itineraries could include the historic cities of Samarkand and Bukhara, as well as Tashkent, the Center of Islamic Civilization and the Imam Bukhari complex.

The sides also identified MICE and industrial tourism as promising areas for cooperation. These could include business events in Uzbekistan and visits to modern enterprises, technology parks and industrial facilities.

''The cooperation is expected to contribute to further growth in mutual tourist flows and strengthen cultural and humanitarian ties between the two countries,'' the Uzbek Tourism Committee said.

Following the meeting, the Uzbekistan Tourism Committee and the Federation of Independent Trade Unions of Russia signed an agreement on cooperation in tourism.

The agreement provides for the development of special tour packages, direct links between trade unions and tourism organizations, familiarization trips and joint promotion of Uzbekistan's tourism opportunities in Russia.

The agreement could provide Uzbekistan with an additional channel for attracting organized groups of Russian tourists, while allowing Russian trade union members to access tailored travel programs covering leisure, health, culture and pilgrimage.

The initiative comes as Uzbekistan seeks to diversify its tourism offerings and strengthen cooperation with Russia, one of the country's key tourism markets.

Azerbaijan’s national team won three bronze medals at the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI 2026), held in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, from 9 to 16 August.

The bronze medalists are Hasan Valiyev, an 11th-grade student at Baku Secondary School No. 157; Akbar Ahmadov, a 10th-grade student at the Baku Physics, Mathematics and Informatics Lyceum; and Ahmad Gambarli, an 11th-grade student at the Baku Turkish Anadolu Lyceum.

Since 2017, “Azercell Telecom” LLC, Ministry of Science and Education of the Republic of Azerbaijan and the Institute of Education have partnered to prepare students for International Olympiads in Informatics. World.title: Turkmenistan advances oil development with new producing wells
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 19. Turkmenistan's Korpedzhe Drilling Operations Department has drilled 11,994 meters and commissioned three oil-producing wells since the beginning of 2026.

The results were announced in a report published by Turkmenistan's state concern Turkmennebit on August 19.

According to the report, all three wells completed over the mentioned period were designed for oil production and demonstrated an industrial flow of crude oil.

The commissioned wells were transferred to the Gumdagnebit Oil and Gas Production Department for further operation.

The drilling specialists used modern equipment to penetrate deeper geological formations and develop hydrocarbon deposits identified by Turkmen geologists, the report noted.

For reference, the Korpedzhe Drilling Operations Department is one of the drilling units of the Nebitgazburawlayysh Trust under Turkmenistan's state concern Turkmennebit. Its main role is to drill oil and gas wells and hand them over to production units for operation. The department operates mainly in western Turkmenistan and has carried out drilling at the Uzynada, Altyguyi, Nogay and Guyjyk fields.

Turkmennebit operates several major oil and gas fields, mainly in the country's Balkan region, including Goturdepe, Barsa-Gelmez, Nebitdag, Korpedzhe, Gamyshlyja, Cheleken and Kemer. The company's drilling units provide new wells for its oil and gas production divisions, making drilling activity an important part of maintaining and expanding domestic hydrocarbon output.

World.title: Iran bars two French diplomats from entering country over alleged misconduct
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 19. Iran has taken diplomatic measures against two employees of the French Embassy in Tehran, declaring them persona non grata and restricting their future entry into the country.

According to Iran’s Foreign Ministry, the decision was linked to what it described as actions by the diplomats that were inconsistent with international law and the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.

The ministry noted that Tehran had informed the French side about the issue several weeks earlier, but no steps were taken to address the situation or prevent similar incidents in the future.

The move follows a statement by Iran’s Intelligence Ministry on August 15, which accused the two French diplomats of involvement in a meeting connected with a case concerning alleged foreign interference.

The ministry claimed that the diplomats had breached Iranian regulations and their diplomatic responsibilities, adding that materials collected during the investigation pointed to broader activities involving covert communications and attempts at external influence.

"The investigation into the case is continuing and that additional information may be released at a later stage," the statement of MFA says. The French government has not yet provided a response to the decision.

World.title: Breaking: Kyrgios tests positive for cocaine in Spain, provisionally suspended
World.content:
Australian tennis star Nick Kyrgios has said he tested positive for cocaine on the Spanish island of Mallorca and has issued an apology.

In a statement on his Instagram, he announced he "made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it".

"I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me," Kyrgios said.

"Above all I'm sorry to the kids who follow me.

"I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed with myself."

The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) issued a statement revealing Kyrgios had been "provisionally suspended" since August 4.

"31-year-old Kyrgios provided a sample during an ATP 250 event in Mallorca, Spain, on 22 June 2026," it said.

"On 17 July 2026, a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory confirmed the presence of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine."

"Kyrgios, who reached a career-high world singles ranking of 13 in October 2016, has the right to appeal the provisional suspension, but has not done so to date," the ITIA said.

"As with all Tennis Anti-Doping Programme cases, ITIA support is available to Kyrgios.

"While suspended, Kyrgios is not allowed to play in, coach at, or attend any events organised or sanctioned by World Tennis, WTA, ATP, the Grand Slams, or any national association."

Kyrgios explained the incident came in the context of years "of injuries... both physically and mentally".

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined."

Kyrgios, 31, has won seven ATP singles titles and the 2022 Australian Open doubles title, partnering with Thanasi Kokkinakis.

World.title: Oil prices spike after ships in Strait of Hormuz hit by fresh strikes
World.content:
Three ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz have been attacked in recent days, British maritime officials said.

The ships were struck by unknown projectiles, resulting in two casualties, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.

INTERCARGO, an association of cargo shipowners, reported that a sailor aboard the Liberian-flagged bulk carrier Minoan Dynasty was killed on Monday.

The Strait of Hormuz saw roughly a fifth of the world's oil pass through it before the war. (ABC News Graphics)

While hostilities between Iran and the United States have eased in recent weeks, a string of attacks on vessels passing through the strait has unsettled investors, pushing oil prices to a three-week high.

Brent crude futures jumped more than 3 per cent over the past week, to $US91.38 by 5:45pm AEST on Friday.

The narrow waterway between Iran and Oman is a vital shipping route for oil in the region.

Amid fresh strikes on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz and stalled peace talks, oil prices have spiked. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Uncertainty over passage through strait

Iran's top negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, said on state media yesterday the strait will remain shut until the US meets the conditions of an interim deal signed between the two countries in June.

The conditions include the US lifting its own blockade, removing oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and ending military threats, he told parliament.

However, last week, Saudi Aramco, the world's top oil producer, resumed loading oil from inside the strait, eyeing Singapore and Malaysia as potential destinations.

Saudi Aramco resumed shipping through the strait last week. (AP: Hassan Ammar)

Despite Iran and the US not directly trading blows, energy prices have remained higher than pre-war levels while the roughly 500 million barrels that usually flow through the strait each month slowed to a trickle.

In a rally speech on Friday, US President Donald Trump said Americans should prepare for higher petrol prices as the war continues.

Shipping through the contested strait has slowed further in recent days, following similar attacks on vessels last week and talks between Iran and the US stalling.

Mr Trump said there are no talks planned between the two countries, and insisted the strait was open.

Donald Trump has repeatedly said throughout the war that the strait is open, saying the US controls the shipping routes. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

"The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated," he said on Truth Social yesterday.

" There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled with the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Naval Blockage remains in full force and effect. "

A ceasefire between Iran and the US expired on Monday, and Mr Trump said he would not be extending it.

The president also said that the US would claim the strait as a US territory after the war.

Trump says Strait of Hormuz to become US territory US President Donald Trump says he will soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, escalating his rhetoric over the vital waterway that carries a significant share of global oil supplies.

Trump upping the rhetoric

The strait is becoming a point of stress for the American president, as the ongoing Iran war becomes increasingly unpopular at home.

He recently threatened to bomb US ally Oman, saying: "If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the shit out of them", in an interview with Fox News.

Oman, whose coastline is a part of the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran have been discussing opening the strait for weeks.

Six months into the conflict, 17 seafarers have died in the waterway according to the UN, with the number of ships passing through estimated to have dropped by roughly 90 per cent.

Many ships travel with their navigation and identification devices turned off to make them harder to attack.

"Seafarers are civilians and must never become targets or collateral victims of geopolitical conflicts," INTERCARGO said in a statement.

" One seafarer lost is one too many. "

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Breaking: 'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident
World.content:
Five Sydney Swans players who were stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards have issued an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

In a statement on behalf of Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner, the players said they were "deeply sorry to everyone involved".

The players were banned by the Swans for breaches of standards and expected behaviour after they stayed out late drinking and brought women back to the team hotel after the game against Essendon on Sunday night.

"We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club," they said.

The five said that they accepted the club's sanction and apologised for the impact on those involved.

Earlier in the day, the Swans said their willingness to "torpedo" their AFL season by suspending the five star players proved their commitment to upholding standards at the club.

In addition to the club sanction, the five Swans players will not be considered for All Australian selection, according to the AFL.

"Following the decision and appropriate club sanction imposed by the Sydney Swans today in relation to the conduct of five of their players, the AFL has determined those players will not be considered for selection in the 2026 All Australian squad," the league said in a statement.

"This decision is independent of the ongoing Victoria Police investigation."

Victorian sex crime detectives are expected to travel to New South Wales as they investigate the alleged incident.

The ABC understands the investigation centres on an allegation of touching without consent at the Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

It is understood the alleged victim has spoken to police.

Multiple law enforcement sources have told the ABC that four officers from the Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad will land in Sydney as they expand their investigation.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges over the alleged incident.

It is not suggested that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault, and none of the banned players has been formally interviewed by police, according to the club.

World.title: Politicians slam 'cruel tool' used to determine at-home aged care funding
World.content:
The federal government is standing by its controversial aged care algorithm, ignoring an offer from the opposition to provide a path through parliament to immediately fix the assessment process at the centre of hundreds of complaints.

Pressure is mounting on Labor over the algorithm after this week's Four Corners investigation, with the Coalition, Greens, independents and some Labor backbenchers, who did not want to be named, demanding the algorithm be either scrapped or urgently fixed.

Shadow Aged Care Minister Anne Ruston secured support when she introduced the bill in the Senate, aiming to overhaul what she labelled a "cruel tool" used to determine how much funding Support at Home recipients received by adding the ability for a human to override assessments.

While the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) involves input from clinicians filling out a questionnaire about the older person, controversially, assessors cannot override the algorithm's final decision on a participant's funding.

Anne Ruston says there is no evidence to prove the tool is working. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Experts, doctors and aged providers have all raised problems with this, including Australia's pre-eminent expert on health care algorithms, Kathy Eagar, who told Four Corners the algorithm needed to be completely ditched.

Last week, the Coalition criticised Labor for shutting down debate on the bill when it moved to the lower house.

"Labor could put human override back into aged care assessments today, by passing our private senator's bill in the House of Representatives," Senator Ruston said.

"Instead they blocked it even being debated, despite the fact it was supported by the Coalition, the Greens, and the crossbench."

Despite acknowledging there had been "confronting" cases, the government is resisting calls to allow human override, insisting the system is working quickly, fairly and has led to only a small number of review requests.

In the first five months of the algorithm's use, more than 1,000 people have asked for their outcome to be reviewed, with 207 people successfully receiving a reassessment.

Inside the aged care algorithm Four Corners reveals the fullest picture yet of the secretive algorithm affecting the lives of tens of thousands of older Australians and their families.

Labor has previously announced it would set up a new "escalation option" so people in "extenuating circumstances" could request their outcome be changed, after the ABC first exposed concerns about the algorithm in March.

Legislation to enact the escalation option has not yet been introduced.

The government is also reviewing the priority system used to determine how quickly someone receives their approved funding, but is not looking into the classification algorithm.

Senator Ruston said what had been announced was not good enough.

"We need more than a so-called 'rapid review' into just one aspect of the faceless algorithm," she said.

"Just as Professor Kathy Eagar AM says, the assessment algorithm is beyond repair, it needs throwing out and starting again.

"Until the government commits to that, older Australians cannot have confidence they will get the care they need."

Crossbenchers slam algorithm in joint statement

Monday's episode of Four Corners also prompted a Greens motion in the Senate calling on the government to replace the IAT with a system that "reinstate[s] the ability for human override".

The motion was backed by the Coalition and crossbenchers, including from the Greens, One Nation and independents.

"We know that this … tool is consistently under-assessing older people's care needs, and we know from the answers that the minister continues to give, that the government is not fully alive to the issue," Greens senator Penny Allman Payne told the Senate.

Senator Ruston said there was "not one piece of evidence" to suggest the tool was working.

"A cruel tool, that this government refuses to acknowledge, is causing older Australians to die unnecessarily," she said on Tuesday.

Independent MP Andrew Wilkie said his office had been contacted by "perplexed and distressed" older Australians struggling to understand the outcomes.

"If the minister thinks this tool is working well, he has his head in the sand," he said.

Monique Ryan is among the crossbenchers who fear the tool is inadequate. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Fellow independent Monique Ryan was worried the tool could amount to a repeat of Robodebt.

"The government's use of algorithms in aged care and the NDIS raises significant concerns around a repeat of the tragedies of Robodebt," she said.

"We can't allow that."

Minister defends tool to deliver 'predictability and consistency'

Despite the mounting pressure and saying the ABC had shared "confronting stories," Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler said he remained a "strong supporter" of the assessment framework.

"[The tool] didn't drop from the sky," he said.

"We're doing everything that we can to make sure this tool delivers the sort of predictability and consistency that the Royal Commission recommended."

In 2021, the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety recommended "a single assessment process based upon a common assessment framework and arrangements [be] followed by all assessors".

The Integrated Assessment Tool (recreated in these images) contains more than 500 questions. (Four Corners: Nick Wiggins)

Mr Butler said he supported a system "that gives confidence to Australians that no matter where they live, no matter what particular assessor organisation that they use, that their package level will reflect their level of need".

But former acting inspector-general of aged care Ian Yates said in his response that Mr Butler had "avoided" dealing with questions about the algorithm.

"The system as it's set up now, which was not as it was recommended by the Royal Commission, will continue to produce Audrey's and all the other cases that were featured in the Four Corners story," he said.

"It's about budgetary control rather than about person-centred care."

Mr Butler said there was still "a very significant role of clinical assessors through this process".

While the government said the IAT allowed for standardised decision making, some Labor MPs have told the ABC they were facing heat from constituents over the system and had raised concerns with Aged Care Minister Sam Rae.

Government follows up cases of participants who spoke out

The Four Corners episode aired a story of a frail 96-year-old who was rejected from receiving more funding to help her pay for the rising cost of in-home care because of an outcome reached by the algorithm.

Sean Dorney was a roaming ABC reporter. Now, just getting out of bed is a struggle A long-time ABC reporter is one of nearly 100,000 Australians waiting on a crucial aged-care assessment.

Under questioning from Liberal Senator Richard Colbeck on Tuesday, Labor's Penny Wong said Audrey Staniland's inability to get more funding sounded "extremely distressing" and the minister had asked the department to look into her case.

One of the other Australians at the centre of the expose on Monday, Sean Dorney, has been told after eight months he would be reassessed for more funding after his decision to speak out.

In the first five months of the algorithm's use, more than 1,000 people have asked for their outcome to be reviewed, with 207 people successful.

World.title: Planners knock back controversial plan for new Bunnings megastore
World.content:
Planning authorities have rejected a fiercely contested multimillion-dollar Bunnings development 10km from its existing site in the West Australian regional city of Bunbury.

A public outcry erupted over the hardware giant's plans to vacate its site at a retail centre in Bunbury, south of Perth, and shift to the town centre of Dalyellup, 10 kilometres away in the neighbouring Shire of Capel.

Bunbury's business and political leaders united in a heated campaign against the new store, arguing it would undermine the viability of the regional centre, and take up land intended for housing.

Opponents to the plan say this vacant land would be better used for housing. (ABC News: Madigan Landry )

After considering the matter for more than four hours, the WA Planning Commission on Wednesday said the Dalyellup block had been identified for residential development and it was not satisfied a big-box retail development represented the "highest and best use" of the land.

Bunnings property and store development manager Garry Hames said he was disappointed by the decision.

"We will take some time to review the outcome and consider our next steps," he said.

A tough decision

Bunnings' current Bunbury landlord, Citygate, told WA planning officials the move would have cost local retailers in lost sales.

Bunnings representatives contested the claim, citing its own projections of a five per cent reduction in turnover for the Bunbury commercial precinct, which it said would be short-term, and affect only larger retailers.

The WA Planning Commission said the proposal was a clear departure from the existing structure plan, in which the land was identified for residential development.

More than 100 people turned out in Bunbury at a public meeting in June to oppose the plan. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Members stressed that this did not mean the land could not be rezoned commercial, but they could not approve the development in its current form.

WA Planning Commission chairperson Emma Cole described it as a challenging application, which was "line ball."

"There have been many valid points raised along the way, and it's certainly been one of the more challenging applications," she said.

Housing concerns

Several deputations were read out to planning officials, raising concerns about the use of land that could otherwise be used for housing.

Among the critics was Anglicare regional manager Lisa Whittaker.

"It removes crucial residential housing land at a time when people are experiencing housing stress, housing instability and homelessness," she said.

Bunnings wanted to build a megastore on this site. (ABC News: Madigan Landry )

Property developer Justin Trewren from Summit Homes said there was a critical land shortage in the South West.

"This removes more than 100 residential shovel-ready lots from the market in the middle of a housing crisis," he said.

But Bunnings and the Shire of Capel strongly rejected claims of harm to housing supply.

Bunnings planning consultant Daniel Lewis said knocking back the proposal would not result in more housing.

The vacant site, south-west of the Bussell Highway roundabout, where Bunnings planned to build a new store. (Supplied: Nearmap)

"[We have] a strong view it was not suitable for housing — the land owner never intended to use it for housing. It would have been a church," he said.

World.title: Claims blowout hits Tasmanian workers' compensation scheme
World.content:
The amount the Tasmanian government has paid for workers' compensation claims has more than tripled over the past decade.

According to the Tasmanian Risk Management Fund's annual reports, the amount the government paid in workers' compensation rose from $32.7 million to $143.4 million between the 2015 and 2024 financial years.

Meanwhile, the government has flagged 1,700 job cuts across the state service.

Tasmania's workers' compensation scheme covers people who have suffered a physical or psychosocial injury, or a disease in the course of their employment, or when their work has substantially contributed to such harm.

A KPMG report found that frontline workers — including police, fire fighters and paramedics — accounted for up to 23 per cent of mental health claims. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Independent body WorkCover Board Tasmania is currently reviewing the scheme to ensure it is fair and financially sustainable.

"The review comes at a time of increasing complexity across workers' compensation systems nationally, including growth in psychological injury claims, increasing claim duration and complexity, and evolving workforce structures," its media release said.

Consultation on the changes closes in September.

Better prevention, support needed

The review has raised concerns for some.

In state parliament on Wednesday, Labor leader Josh Willie asked the treasurer what changes were being considered.

"Will you guarantee that no injured Tasmanian worker will recover a lower payment, lose coverage, or face a higher barrier to make a claim as a result of your review?" he asked.

Treasurer Eric Abetz sought to ease concern, pointing to other states that were reviewing rules around workers' compensation.

"Why would you look to lock in a position before you get a full report, and you've got the information before you to make a genuine considered decision?" Mr Abetz asked.

"What we want to do is get the best possible protection of our workers while the system is sustainable."

Unions Tasmania secretary Jessica Munday said any change that reduced compensation could be detrimental.

She said prioritising preventative measures was more important.

"Resourcing workers, supporting workers, preventing bullying and harassment ... If we invest in those things, we will go a long way towards lowering the cost of workers' compensation," she said.

Jessica Munday says any change to reduced compensation could be detrimental. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Reduced cover not ruled out

Mr Abetz said psychosocial injury claims had doubled over the past decade, and amounted to eight times the cost of a physical injury claim.

Retired police officers lambast minister for trauma support delay Tasmania's association of retired police officers has questioned the police minister over his commitment to the wellbeing of members after the stalling of a much-awaited trial that would offer trauma support.

In 2019, workers' compensation laws were amended in Tasmania so that the cause of the post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) would be automatically presumed to be work-related for the purposes of a compensation claim.

Health Minister Bridget Archer would not rule out the government reducing, narrowing or removing the presumptive cover offered to first responders.

A report by KPMG stated that in the 2024–2025 financial year, 28 per cent of Tasmania's state service claims were mental-health related, and 15 per cent of those were PTSD claims.

It found that frontline workers — including police, firefighters and paramedics — accounted for up to 23 per cent of mental health claims, and that over the past five years the figure appeared to be growing.

The parliament also heard that a specialist wellbeing unit for Department of Justice staff was to be abolished, with the opposition claiming 200 workers would be affected.

Justice Minister Guy Barnett said the change would occur later this year, following a review of wellbeing services.

Bridget Archer would not rule out the government reducing, narrowing or removing the presumptive cover offered to first responders. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Munday criticised this approach.

"That to me sounds like a government that wants to tick off numbers on a budget paper and say 'we have got less staff here', but your costs are going to come out somewhere else," she said.

" What we worry about is that the cost is going to come out in more injuries, not less. "

'Bracing' for 'significant increases'

Hobart-based barrister Luke Taylor, who has represented employees and employers in the workers' compensation process, said the Tasmanian government self-insured its workers' compensation risk through its Tasmanian Risk Management Fund (TRMF).

"Each year, the money that each agency [department] is paid out of that fund to meet its workers' compensation exposure is then calculated to produce a premium that department will then pay into the TRMF for the following year," Mr Taylor said.

Luke Taylor says several significant changes to benefits for DPFEM workers have been made in recent years. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

The Department of Police, Fire and Emergency Management (DPFEM) was an example of a costly department for workers' compensation claims.

Earlier this year, the ABC reported that more than 100 police officers at the time were off work on mental health claims.

During Senate estimates, it was revealed that insurance premiums to the TRMF from the DPFEM had risen from $2 million in 2018 to $63 million this year.

"We have done some work around where we think the premium is going to head and we are bracing ourselves for significant increases in [future] years," Police Commissioner Donna Adams said at the time.

Mr Taylor said several significant changes to benefits for DPFEM workers had been made in recent years, which included the presumption of PTSD.

World.title: Feud escalates as artist puts warning on 'racist' statue
World.content:
A controversial art exhibition examining the racial legacy of a heritage-listed statue in a regional Australian town has sparked a feud between the artist and the local council.

The artwork by Sydney-based artist Osvaldo Budet, on display in the Maitland Regional Art Gallery, examines the statue of an African American boy that has stood on the town's high street for more than a century.

The piece is accompanied by text describing the statue as a "racist image" and an example of how "racism is turned into heritage through sentiment".

The collection of artworks forms part of a broader exhibition examining the history, stories and landscapes of the Hunter region. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

The installation drew the ire of Maitland City councillors, with the majority voting in favour of a motion at a meeting last month expressing a "high level of disappointment" in the gallery's decision to display the artwork and reiterating support for the statue.

Before the motion was put to council, a sign was placed in front of the artwork, warning visitors it may offend members of the community who have "long valued and admired" the statue.

Council erected the signage under the direction of the mayor. (Supplied: Osvaldo Budet)

It was later revealed that the sign was erected under the direction of Maitland Mayor Philip Penfold without consultation or prior knowledge of gallery staff.

In an act of performance art, Mr Budet installed his own temporary sign next to the statue itself, warning it may cause offence to passers-by.

Mr Budet has criticised the mayor's decision to place a warning in front of his work, claiming it stifles public debate about the statue's legacy.

"People in power want to tell some part of the story, not the full picture," Mr Budet said.

" [By installing this sign] I'm now responding to their lack of leadership. "

The story of 'Jocko Graves'

According to a heritage report prepared by council, the statue was likely erected in Maitland in the late 1800s to early 1900s and was recently placed on the city's local heritage register.

The statue is an example of a type of hitching post for horses manufactured in the United States in the late 19th century.

They were widely criticised for racially stereotyping African Americans and as a symbol of slavery.

One unconfirmed story behind the statues is that they were made in honour of an African American boy known as Jocko Graves, who died holding the horses of soldiers during the American Revolutionary War.

The statue has sat on Maitland's High Street for more than a century. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

"My work is the result of a long investigation I've been doing about the history of this hitching post," Mr Budet told Paul Culliver on ABC Newcastle Breakfast.

" [The statue] depicts a boy in a servant position following the lead of a white master because the boy was a slave. "

In an act of performance art, Mr Budet erected his own warning sign next to the statue on Maitland's High Street. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

In July, Cr Penfold released a statement which said the artwork did not represent the views of the Maitland community.

"For generations [the statue] has been embraced by children… photographed by families, as a beloved part of Maitland's identity," the statement read.

" The council's view is that the exhibition, which is largely a 4,000 word opinion, is primarily a political statement, rather than a work of art. "

The artwork and the council's decision to erect the warning sign have since sparked a fierce debate within the Maitland community. (ABC Newcastle: Ben Clifford)

The artwork and the council's decision to erect the warning sign have since sparked a fierce debate within the Maitland community.

"I think it should be kept here; there are other things in Maitland that need to be done [rather] than concentrating on something that's been an icon for years," Maitland local Alice Eccles said.

Paterson resident Julie had a different view.

"I walk past it regularly, and I have always felt uncomfortable," she said.

" It reminds me of the atrocities of slavery and it also reminds me of the atrocities of child labour. "

Questions about council overreach

Maitland Councillor Amelia Atkinson said the mayor's intervention raised questions about proper governance and potentially undermined the art gallery's ability to act independently.

"I think that jump to a mayoral intervention is a huge leap and that's what we've got to really consider moving forward, whether that's appropriate or not," she said.

" If this type of intervention in an art exhibition can occur, can the same thing happen to our libraries if a program is in place that council actually don't like? "

Chief executive of Museums & Galleries of NSW Brett Adlington shared similar concerns.

"I think once you start getting these sort of elected officials stepping into the territory of an organisation in how work is interpreted and communicated to the community, it sort of does then start to undermine the role of the organisation," he said.

Cr Penfold refused the ABC's requests for an interview, and instead provided a statement.

"I reject the suggestion that council is trying to stifle public debate," the statement read.

"The exhibition is open and on full display right now, and people are free to see it, discuss it and form their own views."

Cr Penfold said the decision to erect the warning signage was a "limited and proportionate response" and did not prevent the artist from expressing their views.

Maitland Council's general manager said the decision was in line with the rules set out in the NSW Local Government Act.

World.title: Man who beat his partner to death found 'not criminally responsible'
World.content:
The daughter of an Indigenous woman beaten to death by her partner in outback New South Wales says the killing has "dismantled" her family forever.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this article contains the name of a person who has died and the details may be distressing.

Andrew Charles Smith, 50, faced the NSW Supreme Court in Dubbo, where he was found not criminally responsible for the murder of 47-year-old Mavis Stanley in October 2024 due to a mental health impairment.

Justice Peter Hamill found Mr Smith was probably suffering from schizophrenia with a delusional belief system, which meant he could not reason about whether his actions were wrong.

Mavis Stanley is remembered by friends and family as a strong, caring woman with a big heart. (ABC Western Plains: Jennifer McCutcheon)

Ms Stanley's daughter Jennah-Leigh Dungay told the court there were no words in the English dictionary that could describe the "pain, sorrow, hurt and brokenness" caused by her mother's death.

"You have stolen a future that none of us will ever get to experience," she said.

"My mother was the matriarchal protector of our family, the strength when it was needed and not needed."

Ms Dungay addressed Mr Smith, who appeared in the Dubbo courtroom via audio-visual link.

"The extent of the damage caused is unforgivable, unjust, uncultured and in its shortest form a pure evil," she said.

"We are told it took 15 minutes of brutality using weapons to end my mother's life.

The body of Mavis Stanley was discovered outside her home on October 29. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

"Fifteen minutes to dismantle our family's and friends' hearts forever."

Ms Dungay said she had experienced significant mental health impacts since her mother's death and wanted to see laws strengthened to protect women and children, particularly Indigenous people.

"When a woman has a daughter, she creates a version of her heart that walks in physical form," she told the court.

"So long as I breathe and live, she will speak and live through me.

"Her physical body you may have taken from us, but you will never take her spirit, soul and memory and laughter she left within each of us."

A homicide investigation was launched after a woman's body was found at Bourke, in the NSW north west. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

Accused suffering delusional beliefs

The court heard Mr Smith and Ms Stanley were living in Bourke when, some time between October 26 and 29, he struck her multiple times with a rod-like object, inflicting blunt force injuries that caused her death.

Mr Smith later moved Ms Stanley's body from the home and left her on the roadway.

Two forensic psychiatrists assessed Mr Smith and agreed he was experiencing delusions around the time of Ms Stanley's death.

Listening-device recordings from his prison cell captured Mr Smith speaking to a deity and, on other occasions, apparently to his dead partner.

"Lord you set my life up for failure … I love my wife my Lord … then the devil came up and ripped the heart right out of my chest," he was recorded saying.

Justice Hamill said the recordings showed Mr Smith was "very unwell", thought-disordered and delusional, and may have been experiencing auditory hallucinations.

The judge said he had carefully considered the couple's history of domestic violence and Mr Smith's controlling behaviour.

But he accepted the psychiatrists' evidence that his beliefs about Ms Stanley's infidelity were driven by delusions.

Ms Stanley was found dead outside her home in Bourke, about 370 kilometres from Dubbo. (ABC Western Plains: Zaarkacha Marlan)

"I am satisfied that his preoccupation with Ms Stanley's perceived infidelity was born not of a rational but wicked jealousy, but rather was … the product of his disordered thought processes and delusions at the time of the killing," Justice Hamill said.

He found Mr Smith did not understand his actions were wrong and entered the special verdict.

Justice Hamill acknowledged the words "not criminally responsible" could appear difficult or unjust to Ms Stanley's family, but stressed the verdict did not mean Mr Smith would be released.

'Our hearts are broken'

Several members of Ms Stanley's family travelled to court to deliver victim impact statements, describing her as a strong and fiercely loyal woman who was deeply connected to her family.

Her relatives told the court they had struggled with grief, sleeplessness and fear since her death, and had become increasingly vigilant about the safety of women in their family.

In one statement, Ms Stanley was remembered as "one of a kind" with a "big heart", whose death had left a piece of the family's hearts that would never mend.

Another statement described the 47-year-old as the "rock" of her family, with a "wicked sense of humour" and a laugh her loved ones could still hear.

The court heard her family had been unable to prepare and farewell Ms Stanley's body in accordance with their cultural practices because of the extent of her injuries.

Justice Hamill praised the family's courage and dignity throughout the proceedings.

"These statements will remain on the court's records and archives as an enduring testament to a remarkable woman whose life was taken too soon and by violence," he said.

World.title: Swans players could face up to $600,000 sponsorship hit
World.content:
A raft of the Swans’ biggest sponsors have declared they take have no tolerance for wrongdoing after Telstra stood down brand ambassadors Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner following breaches of club behaviour standards on Sunday night. That night is also the subject of an investigation into an allegation of sexual assault by one woman. If the accusations are proven and sponsors flee, marketing experts have warned that Heeney alone could face a $600,000 income hit from losing his personal backers, along with those that have put the Swans as a club on notice. Sydney Swans players Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey. Marija Ercegovac Insurance giant QBE, property listings company realestate.com.au, Origin Energy and Hong Kong sauce giant Lee Kum Kee are among the brands that have expressed concern, while other sponsors such as Nike and McDonalds have either declined to comment or not responded. When Telstra stood down Heeney and Warner from the telecommunication giant’s brand ambassador program on Monday, it also expressed its deep concern at the police investigation.



“We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time,” Telstra’s spokeswoman said. Victoria Police are investigating a woman’s allegation that she was sexually assaulted in the early hours of Monday morning at the Pullman Hotel. Sources said she had alleged she was touched beyond what had been previously agreed. Heeney is said to be a focus of the investigation. None of the players involved has been formally interviewed by police, and there is no suggestion that the allegations are correct, only that they were made by the woman. Telstra had recently featured Heeney in campaigns based around community initiatives including grassroots football and mental-health programs. Five Swans players – Heeney, Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon – were suspended by the club for the remainder of the season on Wednesday morning for breaching club behaviour standards.



The players issued a joint statement on Wednesday apologising for their behaviour, which they said had let down their families, supporters, colleagues in the AFLW and wider community. Related Article Crime Isaac Heeney revealed as player at centre of sexual assault investigation “We accept the club sanction and apologise for the impact this has had on those involved,” the players’ statement reads. “Our focus will now be on rebuilding trust with the club and the community.” A source familiar with the players’ thinking said they denied any criminal wrongdoing. The incident threatens to compromise the Swans’ hard-cultivated identity as a progressive-minded club known for promoting women’s and LGBTQI rights.



Global marketing strategist Toby Ralph, who has previously run major political campaigns for the Liberal party among other causes, said: “The club has very deliberately sold respect, inclusion and the advancement of women as part of its institutional identity.” “When your behaviour contradicts your advertising, a scandal becomes a brand problem,” Ralph said. He said that while this week’s news would hurt the Swans brand, the club’s reputation was salvageable. “In some respects their decision to dump five important players for the rest of the season, potentially damaging a premiership campaign, is exactly what a values-based brand is supposed to do. Values only become values when they cost you something.” The Swans are the 3rd most valuable AFL club, with a value of $115 million, according to research from consultancy Brand Finance Australia.



Ralph estimated that Heeney, who is one of the AFL’s most marketable stars, could take home up to $250,000 a year from a single major sponsor, and up to $600,000 across a portfolio of deals. The Swans star recently released a series of children’s books called Little Isaac Footy Fever, co-authored with writer Nicole Hayes. Related Article Analysis

AFL off-field behaviour Brace yourselves: The finals won’t be a consideration for Sydney Publisher Allen & Unwin did not respond to comment requests. Online book retailer Booktopia said it was assessing the situation. “Our mandate is to provide a service and selection of books in the best interest of our customers,” a spokesman said. “We appreciate the sensitivity and will carefully consider any decision, together with the publisher, in due course.”



Several key Swans sponsors have released statements noting the serious allegations facing the club. Insurer QBE, which is the longstanding principal sponsor of the Swans’ mens and women’s teams, said it “acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported”. “We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club’s position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women,” a spokesperson said. “Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further.” A spokesperson for Realestate.com.au, which is a major partner, said the company was “deeply concerned by the serious allegations”. “We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations,” they said.



On Tuesday, a spokesperson for Origin Energy expressed disappointment. “The club informed us about this incident yesterday, and we are incredibly disappointed. While the matter is subject to an investigation, it is not appropriate for us to comment any further,” they said. A spokesperson for Hong Kong-based condiment manufacturer Lee Kum Kee, which is also a partner, said that the company took personal safety and wellbeing seriously. “At this point we are not in a position to comment on the details of any alleged incident or the status of any investigation,” they said. Mashoom Tait, chief executive of Adelaide Hills winery Bird in Hand, an official partner, said the company was aware of the “serious allegations” but declined to comment further given the ongoing investigation. Other major club sponsors including Nike, McDonalds and Vokswagen either declined to comment or did not respond to enquiries.
