World.title: ‘A portrait in music’: Elite violinist pays tribute to his beloved teacher
World.content:
NationalVictoriaLive music ‘A portrait in music’: Elite violinist pays tribute to his beloved teacher Carolyn Webb August 19, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

He’s performed on the world’s great stages and worked with Paul McCartney, Burt Bacharach and Sting, but Australian violinist Patrick Savage still gets nervous before a show. As the curtain rises, he remembers a pep talk his childhood violin teacher Donald Scotts gave him when he was 13, before a recital. Saying thanks: International violinist Patrick Savage with the violin his mentor Donald Scotts gave him. Chris Hopkins “He said, ‘You’ve done the work, you’re prepared, and all you have to do is go and enjoy it,’” Savage says. “It’s still something I replay in my head when I’m on stage.”



Savage, who grew up in Bendigo, is lead violinist for the musical Hamilton in London’s West End. He’s a former principal first violin of the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, led Bacharach’s UK touring orchestra and played on two McCartney albums. Loading He composes and plays on Hollywood film soundtracks and has performed at London’s O2 arena and the Lincoln Centre in New York. But Savage is in Victoria on a personal quest – a tribute to his mentor Scotts, in three concerts and a new album.



From the age of six to 18, Savage took private lessons from “Mr Scotts” at the Victorian College of the Arts. Every two weeks, Savage would take a train from Bendigo to Melbourne and back. The lessons ended when Savage went to study at the Royal College of Music in London, but Savage never forgot Scotts. Reunited: Savage (right), during a visit to his mentor Scotts in Rosebud in 2018. “He made an enormous impact on my life,” Savage says. He says Scotts, who had been Melbourne Symphony Orchestra associate concertmaster and had led the Melbourne String Quartet, was a grandfather figure who was “irrepressibly joyful”.



The lessons never felt like a chore. “I wanted to have him praise me,” Savage says. “And have him saying ‘best yet’, which was his slogan, if you’d done well.” Savage strove to play violin like Scotts – with charm, warmth and “this sparkle behind the eyes”. In 2023, in his second to last visit to Scotts’ Rosebud retirement home before Scotts died in 2024 at the age of 97, Savage played some of Scotts’ favourite pieces. Grandfather figure: Scotts embraces Savage on a 2023 visit to Scotts’ Rosebud aged care home. Scotts’ daughter is in the background. Scotts then presented Savage with his own childhood violin and his sheet music collection with personal notations.



Savage says he was so moved he couldn’t speak. His album Encores for Mr Scotts, with Savage on violin and Martin Cousin on piano, and the concerts with pianist Coady Green – on August 30 at Langley Estate in Bendigo, on September 3 at Brunswick venue Tempo Rubato and on September 5 at Christ Church in Daylesford – are “a thank-you to Don”. Each piece he will play is “meaningful somehow, or says something about him”. A life’s collection: Some of the sheet music Scotts gave his former violin student Savage in 2023. They include Jota by Manuel de Falla, which Savage played at 13, when Scotts gave him the pep talk; Fritz Kreisler’s Tempo di Minuetto – “rousing, charming, energetic, like Don and that he played beautifully”; and Mantle of Blue, a folk lullaby by a favourite composer of Scotts’, Ernest John Moeran.



“I thought, ‘How can I do a portrait of Don in music?’” Savage says, to sum up the project. “I want more people to know about Don Scotts, to do my small part to put his name out there again.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Caught in a car in a flood? Don’t believe what you see on TV
World.content:
While Peden’s primary piece of advice is to avoid floodwater at all costs , she acknowledges that it’s not always a question of choice: fatal floods, which Peden says are increasing due to climate change , can often come out of nowhere. “Moving water is conceptually hard to comprehend,” she says. “It’s very difficult for most of us to assess water depth and velocity.”

If you’re a fan of action movies, you may think that the celluloid version of a car being submerged in water – after flying off a pier in slo-mo, or somersaulting off a bridge during a high-octane shootout – reflects what happens in real life. But, in reality, you’re far more likely to find your vehicle trapped in water in the context of a flood. “ At least half the drowning deaths that happen in floods are vehicle-related ,” says Dr Amy Peden, a drowning prevention researcher at UNSW. “A lot of people have this misconception that your car has to be fully submerged for drowning to occur.”

Each week, Good Weekend’s how-to column shares expert advice on how to navigate some of modern life’s big – and small – challenges. This week: How to get out of a car in floodwater.

Fifteen to 20 centimetres of water are sufficient to float a car: “Once it’s under all four wheels, you’ve lost contact with the road and control of your vehicle,” she says. This is where things can get gnarly. Conventional wisdom would say this is the point at which you dial for help, but this prioritising could push you further into dire straits. “That time is probably better spent trying to get on top of the vehicle, into a tree or to the riverbank,” Peden says. “Emergency services will likely be inundated with other calls; you might not even have a signal.”

How you exit the car is vitally important. Electric windows will stop working within a minute of water reaching the switches. “Everyone should have [a glass breaker] in their car,” Peden says (these are inexpensive and available online: some models helpfully include a seatbelt cutter).

Use it to smash a side window (not the windshield or rear window) by hitting it very hard at any one of its four corners. Complete the action-hero manoeuvre by escaping through it quickly: vehicles can go from floating to fully submerged in seconds.

Never open a door, particularly if you’re in deeper water: “You want to avoid, as much as possible, filling the car with water and speeding up the sinking process,” says Peden. And don’t believe what you see on TV, where commercials can glorify the ability of a vehicle to make it through floodwaters.

“People overestimate the ability of their vehicle to go through water because they’ve seen it in an ad,” she says. “The party line really is, ‘If it’s flooded, forget it.’ ”

World.title: The six signs of good mental health, according to psychologists
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsWellness The six signs of good mental health, according to psychologists Abby Seaman August 19, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s often tempting to dwell on the negative, especially when it comes to mental health. The signs of mental illness, like depression or anxiety, are often the focus when we talk about our psychological wellbeing. But what about the positives? Psychologist Chris Cheers says the term mental health itself carries a negative connotation. “Nobody takes a ‘mental health day’ because things are going brilliantly. That tells us something,” Cheers says. Good mental wellbeing includes doing lots of little habits every day. Getty Images A more helpful framework is thinking of our mental healthcare as an ongoing process of small daily habits.



So, we asked experts to tell us the signs and habits commonly associated with good mental health. You have a morning and evening routine Cheers says you can’t control your day, but you can have some autonomy over its start and end. “I don’t just mean waking up or going to bed at a specific time. I mean having little rituals that set you up for a good day, and a good sleep,” he says. In the morning, Cheers explains, you might prioritise writing in a journal, listening to music while having your coffee or doing some stretching.



Related Article Exclusive

Parenting Can mothers prevent passing on mental illness? This new study offers insight “For an evening routine, it’s anything that helps you wind down: tea, calling a friend, reading, deep breathing. “These routines matter because the more predictability you bring into your day, the calmer your nervous system becomes,” Cheers says. But maintaining regular sleep times can also be beneficial. A 2025 study found that people consistent in bed and wake times had a 38 per cent lower risk of depression and 33 per cent lower risk of anxiety compared to irregular sleepers.



You check in with yourself Related Article Wellbeing Does the body keep the score? Our brains and bodies are more linked than we knew Doing a regular check-in with your body is an easy way to see if it is telling you something, particularly when life gets busy or if you have been taught to avoid giving certain emotions airtime. “I teach almost every client – and use myself – what I call a ‘body check-in’. You take a breath, bring your attention to your body, and ask three questions: How do I feel? Why does it make sense that I feel like that? What do I need?” Cheers says. Listening to and trusting your body is a step towards good mental health, he says.



You’re compassionate Katie Dobinson, a clinical psychologist at This Way Up at St Vincent’s Health Network Sydney, says an indicator of good wellbeing is unique to individuals and their circumstances. “Maintaining one’s mental health helps to prevent mental illness and worsening quality of life,” Dobinson says. One example, she suggests, is having compassion for yourself when you make a mistake. This also includes letting yourself ask for support when you need it. Prioritising healthy relationships and community is essential to good mental health. Getty Images



You have a sense of purpose Dobinson says it’s important to have a sense of purpose or meaning in life. Research shows that people who feel a sense of purpose in their life deal better with stress and are more likely to experience greater mental health. “This could look like working towards a new goal at work, maintaining connection with loved ones, pursuing learning and knowledge, or practising a new skill,” Dobinson says. “[Or] being able to engage in both essential and meaningful activities. This may be in daily self-care activities, engaging in meaningful study, work or volunteering, or pursuing tasks that matter to you.”





A 2023 study published by Nature Medicine suggests that engaging in a hobby is good for your wellbeing. Researchers analysed studies involving more than 93,000 people across 16 countries and found those with hobbies reported better health, including fewer symptoms of depression. “Good mental health involves social connection,” Dobinson says. You’re realistic Being realistic includes being realistic about your mental health and goal setting. “Being realistic and balanced with your thinking. This can often involve being able to identify unhelpful thinking patterns and learning to see things from a balanced perspective,” Dobinson says.



It also means you have good and bad days; you can’t completely avoid negative or anxious thoughts. And realistic planning means you have something to look forward to. “Having goals and plans for the future increases our motivation, brings us happiness, and helps to focus our mind on important tasks. Planning things to look forward to, or setting a goal to overcome a past challenge, can be healthy ways to improve your general wellbeing,” Dobinson says. You have coping strategies It’s human to experience difficult emotions or setbacks, Dobinson says, but if you have a mental tool kit of coping strategies, it’s a sign of generally healthy mental wellbeing. Fostering a sense of resilience can help you cope with life’s difficulties.



Related Article Wellbeing It turns out this universal guilty pleasure is actually good for our health “This doesn’t mean you don’t experience negative emotions or stress, but that you’re able to navigate these stressors, ask for help, and adjust over time,” Dobinson says. Another indicator is being comfortable seeking support from a health professional when needed. So never be afraid to ask for help. Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Kyrgios tests positive to cocaine, faces lengthy ban from tennis
World.content:
Breaking SportTennisDrugs in sport Kyrgios tests positive to cocaine, faces lengthy ban from tennis Marc McGowan August 19, 2026 — 6:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Controversial Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios has taken full responsibility for making a “huge mistake” after testing positive for banned substance cocaine. The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) announced on Wednesday night (AEST) that it had provisionally suspended Kyrgios under the tennis anti-doping program. He has so far not appealed the decision. Nick Kyrgios is a former world No.13 who reached the 2022 men’s singles final at Wimbledon. Marijan Murat/Picture Alliance via Getty Images The 31-year-old provided a sample during an ATP 250 event in Mallorca, Spain, on June 22 before a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory confirmed the presence of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine, on July 17. Kyrgios’ provisional suspension started on August 4.



Related Article Wimbledon Kyrgios drama as he bids Wimbledon farewell; doubt surrounds Serena In a statement posted to his Instagram story on Wednesday, Kyrgios apologised for his actions and said he would take a break from social media and public life to “focus on getting myself right”. “I wanted you to hear this from me first. I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine,” Kyrgios posted. “I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it. I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets, and I’m deeply disappointed in myself. “I’m not going to make excuses, but I do want to give some context about where I’ve been. The last couple of years of injuries have taken a huge toll on me, both physically and mentally.



Nick Kyrgios’ apology on his official Instagram account. Instagram “My body hasn’t been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined. “I’ve always said I didn’t choose tennis – tennis chose me. But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I’ve ever had to face. At times I’ve felt helpless and alone. None of that excuses what I did. “However, the good news is that this has given me a wake-up call. For the next 28 days, I’ll be stepping away from social media and public life while I focus on getting myself right. “I’d ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly, the privacy of my family. I’m sorry. I’ll do the work and come back better.”



According to the ITIA, Kyrgios, the former world No.13 and 2022 Wimbledon finalist, is yet to appeal the provisional suspension. This masthead has contacted Kyrgios’ management. More to come

World.title: Governor-general ‘shocked and troubled’ by Swans sexual assault allegation
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAFL off-field behaviour Governor-general ‘shocked and troubled’ by Swans sexual assault allegation Natassia Chrysanthos August 19, 2026 — 6:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s Governor-General Sam Mostyn has said she is shocked and troubled by the alleged sexual assault investigation that has engulfed the Sydney Swans while warning that a lack of respect for women across the country remained a problem, particularly in sport. In a rare intervention from a head of state, Mostyn said that sports clubs and the community in general needed to be vigilant about women’s treatment while noting Australia still had “appalling statistics” when it came to domestic and sexual violence against women. Governor-General Sam Mostyn. Alex Ellinghausen Five Sydney Swans players were on Wednesday suspended for the rest of the season for breach of club behavioural standards as Victoria Police started investigating separate conduct of an allegation of sexual assault from Sunday night. A woman provided a written complaint to city police on Tuesday afternoon, although no charges have yet been laid. “I was shocked and troubled by the allegation of sexual assault … stemming from the weekend in Melbourne,” Ms Mostyn said, in comments first reported by the ABC on Wednesday evening.



“At times like this, we are reminded to never take for granted the need for constant vigilance for respectful treatment of women everywhere; across clubs, the AFL, sport, and the community generally. “The most important thing in moments like this is to fully accept responsibility, be accountable and take appropriate action.” Mostyn, a prominent businesswoman, became the first female member of the AFL commission in 2005 and joined the Swans board in 2017. She resigned from that position when Prime Minister Anthony Albanese appointed her as Australia’s 28th governor-general in 2024. She has commented on gender equality issues since taking the role, after a corporate career that often highlighted women’s issues. Last month, Mostyn publicly backed quotas to install more women in senior roles. However, she has typically refrained from discussing controversies or sensitive matters that are open to investigation, and it is extremely rare for a governor-general to comment on such issues. Mostyn said her thoughts were with the woman who made the sexual assault allegation, and that she hoped she was being supported.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Deeply sorry to everyone involved’: Suspended Swans speak out for first time “I am also devastated for the women of the Swans, whether they are players, staff, fans and everyone involved in the club and women across the industry who have been hurt by this incident,” she said. “Sadly, the lack of respect for women across the country remains an issue for us all to be concerned about, particularly in sport. We must all, men and women, constantly strive for respect for everyone, to educate our youngest players and fans, and that responsibility to educate is held by so many; administrators, leaders and players of the sport, all of whom shape culture. “I note Australia still has appalling statistics when it comes to domestic and sexual violence against women.” Mostyn said she believed great progress had been made to make sure women were represented in sport, particularly in women’s leagues.



“We have seen this magnificent and timely inclusion and celebration of women across our football codes, and today, little boys and girls know women are welcome and respected across our sporting landscape,” she said. But she said Australia needed to “remain committed to bringing more women into positions of influence in the AFL and all sports”, citing her own experience of joining the AFL commission as instructive in demonstrating why it was important to bring a woman’s perspective to the game. “We need more women inside the game, from coaching, administration, leadership and governance. And that’s also across all sport. The more diverse and representative people are in club culture and sports culture, the greater confidence we can have in safe places for women, and everyone,” she said. Mostyn said she had committed herself “to put care, kindness and respect at the centre of my work when I became governor-general”. Related Article Crime Isaac Heeney revealed as player at centre of sexual assault investigation



“I believe that is what most Australians want all our leaders and role models to show; that everyone can feel respected, welcome and safe in any workplace, sporting, or community context,” she said. “But again we must ensure that women are present and valued for their insights, experience and contribution to establishing respectful environments, at all levels of leadership, coaching, administration. Sport must be a safe place for everybody. Particularly women in the football codes. “We all have a duty to call out bad behaviour whenever we see it and always encourage and teach what respectful behaviour requires of us all.” Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek on Wednesday afternoon said she did not want to speak about individual cases, but said sporting codes should know how powerful their voices were. “I want to be very careful not to speak about any of the allegations or investigations underway in specific terms … I don’t want to prejudice any potential investigation,” she said on the ABC.



“I’d say a few things in general terms. Sporting codes, teams like the Swans have an incredibly important role in our community. They are the people who boys and young men look up to, they’re their heroes, they’re role models. And I am really pleased to hear some of the measures that the club’s taken today. “I think it is important to show that sporting clubs, schools, other institutions take allegations of sexual assault seriously. It is really important that in any discussion we centre victims and survivors of sexual assault. And hearing the club take strong measures is a really important step forward.” The Swans released a statement on behalf of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice on Wednesday evening. “We are deeply sorry to everyone involved. We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club,” the statement read. “We know we have let down our partners and families, members, supporters, teammates, the AFLW team, corporate partners and everyone at the club and the wider community. We accept the club sanction and apologise for the impact this has had on those involved. Our focus will now be on rebuilding trust with the club and the community.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Swans players could face up to $600,000 sponsorship hit
World.content:
A raft of the Swans’ biggest sponsors have declared they take have no tolerance for wrongdoing after Telstra stood down brand ambassadors Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner following breaches of club behaviour standards on Sunday night. That night is also the subject of an investigation into an allegation of sexual assault by one woman. If the accusations are proven and sponsors flee, marketing experts have warned that Heeney alone could face a $600,000 income hit from losing his personal backers, along with those that have put the Swans as a club on notice. Sydney Swans players Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey. Marija Ercegovac Insurance giant QBE, property listings company realestate.com.au, Origin Energy and Hong Kong sauce giant Lee Kum Kee are among the brands that have expressed concern, while other sponsors such as Nike and McDonalds have either declined to comment or not responded. When Telstra stood down Heeney and Warner from the telecommunication giant’s brand ambassador program on Monday, it also expressed its deep concern at the police investigation.



“We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time,” Telstra’s spokeswoman said. Victoria Police are investigating a woman’s allegation that she was sexually assaulted in the early hours of Monday morning at the Pullman Hotel. Sources said she had alleged she was touched beyond what had been previously agreed. Heeney is said to be a focus of the investigation. None of the players involved has been formally interviewed by police, and there is no suggestion that the allegations are correct, only that they were made by the woman. Telstra had recently featured Heeney in campaigns based around community initiatives including grassroots football and mental-health programs. Five Swans players – Heeney, Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon – were suspended by the club for the remainder of the season on Wednesday morning for breaching club behaviour standards.



The players issued a joint statement on Wednesday apologising for their behaviour, which they said had let down their families, supporters, colleagues in the AFLW and wider community. Related Article Crime Isaac Heeney revealed as player at centre of sexual assault investigation “We accept the club sanction and apologise for the impact this has had on those involved,” the players’ statement reads. “Our focus will now be on rebuilding trust with the club and the community.” A source familiar with the players’ thinking said they denied any criminal wrongdoing. The incident threatens to compromise the Swans’ hard-cultivated identity as a progressive-minded club known for promoting women’s and LGBTQI rights.



Global marketing strategist Toby Ralph, who has previously run major political campaigns for the Liberal party among other causes, said: “The club has very deliberately sold respect, inclusion and the advancement of women as part of its institutional identity.” “When your behaviour contradicts your advertising, a scandal becomes a brand problem,” Ralph said. He said that while this week’s news would hurt the Swans brand, the club’s reputation was salvageable. “In some respects their decision to dump five important players for the rest of the season, potentially damaging a premiership campaign, is exactly what a values-based brand is supposed to do. Values only become values when they cost you something.” The Swans are the 3rd most valuable AFL club, with a value of $115 million, according to research from consultancy Brand Finance Australia.



Ralph estimated that Heeney, who is one of the AFL’s most marketable stars, could take home up to $250,000 a year from a single major sponsor, and up to $600,000 across a portfolio of deals. The Swans star recently released a series of children’s books called Little Isaac Footy Fever, co-authored with writer Nicole Hayes. Related Article Analysis

AFL off-field behaviour Brace yourselves: The finals won’t be a consideration for Sydney Publisher Allen & Unwin did not respond to comment requests. Online book retailer Booktopia said it was assessing the situation. “Our mandate is to provide a service and selection of books in the best interest of our customers,” a spokesman said. “We appreciate the sensitivity and will carefully consider any decision, together with the publisher, in due course.”



Several key Swans sponsors have released statements noting the serious allegations facing the club. Insurer QBE, which is the longstanding principal sponsor of the Swans’ mens and women’s teams, said it “acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported”. “We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club’s position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women,” a spokesperson said. “Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further.” A spokesperson for Realestate.com.au, which is a major partner, said the company was “deeply concerned by the serious allegations”. “We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations,” they said.



On Tuesday, a spokesperson for Origin Energy expressed disappointment. “The club informed us about this incident yesterday, and we are incredibly disappointed. While the matter is subject to an investigation, it is not appropriate for us to comment any further,” they said. A spokesperson for Hong Kong-based condiment manufacturer Lee Kum Kee, which is also a partner, said that the company took personal safety and wellbeing seriously. “At this point we are not in a position to comment on the details of any alleged incident or the status of any investigation,” they said. Mashoom Tait, chief executive of Adelaide Hills winery Bird in Hand, an official partner, said the company was aware of the “serious allegations” but declined to comment further given the ongoing investigation. Other major club sponsors including Nike, McDonalds and Vokswagen either declined to comment or did not respond to enquiries.

World.title: ‘A portrait in music’: Elite violinist pays tribute to his beloved teacher
World.content:
NationalVictoriaLive music ‘A portrait in music’: Elite violinist pays tribute to his beloved teacher Carolyn Webb August 19, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

He’s performed on the world’s great stages and worked with Paul McCartney, Burt Bacharach and Sting, but Australian violinist Patrick Savage still gets nervous before a show. As the curtain rises, he remembers a pep talk his childhood violin teacher Donald Scotts gave him when he was 13, before a recital. Saying thanks: International violinist Patrick Savage with the violin his mentor Donald Scotts gave him. Chris Hopkins “He said, ‘You’ve done the work, you’re prepared, and all you have to do is go and enjoy it,’” Savage says. “It’s still something I replay in my head when I’m on stage.”



Savage, who grew up in Bendigo, is lead violinist for the musical Hamilton in London’s West End. He’s a former principal first violin of the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, led Bacharach’s UK touring orchestra and played on two McCartney albums. Loading He composes and plays on Hollywood film soundtracks and has performed at London’s O2 arena and the Lincoln Centre in New York. But Savage is in Victoria on a personal quest – a tribute to his mentor Scotts, in three concerts and a new album.



From the age of six to 18, Savage took private lessons from “Mr Scotts” at the Victorian College of the Arts. Every two weeks, Savage would take a train from Bendigo to Melbourne and back. The lessons ended when Savage went to study at the Royal College of Music in London, but Savage never forgot Scotts. Reunited: Savage (right), during a visit to his mentor Scotts in Rosebud in 2018. “He made an enormous impact on my life,” Savage says. He says Scotts, who had been Melbourne Symphony Orchestra associate concertmaster and had led the Melbourne String Quartet, was a grandfather figure who was “irrepressibly joyful”.



The lessons never felt like a chore. “I wanted to have him praise me,” Savage says. “And have him saying ‘best yet’, which was his slogan, if you’d done well.” Savage strove to play violin like Scotts – with charm, warmth and “this sparkle behind the eyes”. In 2023, in his second to last visit to Scotts’ Rosebud retirement home before Scotts died in 2024 at the age of 97, Savage played some of Scotts’ favourite pieces. Grandfather figure: Scotts embraces Savage on a 2023 visit to Scotts’ Rosebud aged care home. Scotts’ daughter is in the background. Scotts then presented Savage with his own childhood violin and his sheet music collection with personal notations.



Savage says he was so moved he couldn’t speak. His album Encores for Mr Scotts, with Savage on violin and Martin Cousin on piano, and the concerts with pianist Coady Green – on August 30 at Langley Estate in Bendigo, on September 3 at Brunswick venue Tempo Rubato and on September 5 at Christ Church in Daylesford – are “a thank-you to Don”. Each piece he will play is “meaningful somehow, or says something about him”. A life’s collection: Some of the sheet music Scotts gave his former violin student Savage in 2023. They include Jota by Manuel de Falla, which Savage played at 13, when Scotts gave him the pep talk; Fritz Kreisler’s Tempo di Minuetto – “rousing, charming, energetic, like Don and that he played beautifully”; and Mantle of Blue, a folk lullaby by a favourite composer of Scotts’, Ernest John Moeran.



“I thought, ‘How can I do a portrait of Don in music?’” Savage says, to sum up the project. “I want more people to know about Don Scotts, to do my small part to put his name out there again.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Caught in a car in a flood? Don’t believe what you see on TV
World.content:
While Peden’s primary piece of advice is to avoid floodwater at all costs , she acknowledges that it’s not always a question of choice: fatal floods, which Peden says are increasing due to climate change , can often come out of nowhere. “Moving water is conceptually hard to comprehend,” she says. “It’s very difficult for most of us to assess water depth and velocity.”

If you’re a fan of action movies, you may think that the celluloid version of a car being submerged in water – after flying off a pier in slo-mo, or somersaulting off a bridge during a high-octane shootout – reflects what happens in real life. But, in reality, you’re far more likely to find your vehicle trapped in water in the context of a flood. “ At least half the drowning deaths that happen in floods are vehicle-related ,” says Dr Amy Peden, a drowning prevention researcher at UNSW. “A lot of people have this misconception that your car has to be fully submerged for drowning to occur.”

Each week, Good Weekend’s how-to column shares expert advice on how to navigate some of modern life’s big – and small – challenges. This week: How to get out of a car in floodwater.

Fifteen to 20 centimetres of water are sufficient to float a car: “Once it’s under all four wheels, you’ve lost contact with the road and control of your vehicle,” she says. This is where things can get gnarly. Conventional wisdom would say this is the point at which you dial for help, but this prioritising could push you further into dire straits. “That time is probably better spent trying to get on top of the vehicle, into a tree or to the riverbank,” Peden says. “Emergency services will likely be inundated with other calls; you might not even have a signal.”

How you exit the car is vitally important. Electric windows will stop working within a minute of water reaching the switches. “Everyone should have [a glass breaker] in their car,” Peden says (these are inexpensive and available online: some models helpfully include a seatbelt cutter).

Use it to smash a side window (not the windshield or rear window) by hitting it very hard at any one of its four corners. Complete the action-hero manoeuvre by escaping through it quickly: vehicles can go from floating to fully submerged in seconds.

Never open a door, particularly if you’re in deeper water: “You want to avoid, as much as possible, filling the car with water and speeding up the sinking process,” says Peden. And don’t believe what you see on TV, where commercials can glorify the ability of a vehicle to make it through floodwaters.

“People overestimate the ability of their vehicle to go through water because they’ve seen it in an ad,” she says. “The party line really is, ‘If it’s flooded, forget it.’ ”

World.title: The six signs of good mental health, according to psychologists
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsWellness The six signs of good mental health, according to psychologists Abby Seaman August 19, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s often tempting to dwell on the negative, especially when it comes to mental health. The signs of mental illness, like depression or anxiety, are often the focus when we talk about our psychological wellbeing. But what about the positives? Psychologist Chris Cheers says the term mental health itself carries a negative connotation. “Nobody takes a ‘mental health day’ because things are going brilliantly. That tells us something,” Cheers says. Good mental wellbeing includes doing lots of little habits every day. Getty Images A more helpful framework is thinking of our mental healthcare as an ongoing process of small daily habits.



So, we asked experts to tell us the signs and habits commonly associated with good mental health. You have a morning and evening routine Cheers says you can’t control your day, but you can have some autonomy over its start and end. “I don’t just mean waking up or going to bed at a specific time. I mean having little rituals that set you up for a good day, and a good sleep,” he says. In the morning, Cheers explains, you might prioritise writing in a journal, listening to music while having your coffee or doing some stretching.



Related Article Exclusive

Parenting Can mothers prevent passing on mental illness? This new study offers insight “For an evening routine, it’s anything that helps you wind down: tea, calling a friend, reading, deep breathing. “These routines matter because the more predictability you bring into your day, the calmer your nervous system becomes,” Cheers says. But maintaining regular sleep times can also be beneficial. A 2025 study found that people consistent in bed and wake times had a 38 per cent lower risk of depression and 33 per cent lower risk of anxiety compared to irregular sleepers.



You check in with yourself Related Article Wellbeing Does the body keep the score? Our brains and bodies are more linked than we knew Doing a regular check-in with your body is an easy way to see if it is telling you something, particularly when life gets busy or if you have been taught to avoid giving certain emotions airtime. “I teach almost every client – and use myself – what I call a ‘body check-in’. You take a breath, bring your attention to your body, and ask three questions: How do I feel? Why does it make sense that I feel like that? What do I need?” Cheers says. Listening to and trusting your body is a step towards good mental health, he says.



You’re compassionate Katie Dobinson, a clinical psychologist at This Way Up at St Vincent’s Health Network Sydney, says an indicator of good wellbeing is unique to individuals and their circumstances. “Maintaining one’s mental health helps to prevent mental illness and worsening quality of life,” Dobinson says. One example, she suggests, is having compassion for yourself when you make a mistake. This also includes letting yourself ask for support when you need it. Prioritising healthy relationships and community is essential to good mental health. Getty Images



You have a sense of purpose Dobinson says it’s important to have a sense of purpose or meaning in life. Research shows that people who feel a sense of purpose in their life deal better with stress and are more likely to experience greater mental health. “This could look like working towards a new goal at work, maintaining connection with loved ones, pursuing learning and knowledge, or practising a new skill,” Dobinson says. “[Or] being able to engage in both essential and meaningful activities. This may be in daily self-care activities, engaging in meaningful study, work or volunteering, or pursuing tasks that matter to you.”





A 2023 study published by Nature Medicine suggests that engaging in a hobby is good for your wellbeing. Researchers analysed studies involving more than 93,000 people across 16 countries and found those with hobbies reported better health, including fewer symptoms of depression. “Good mental health involves social connection,” Dobinson says. You’re realistic Being realistic includes being realistic about your mental health and goal setting. “Being realistic and balanced with your thinking. This can often involve being able to identify unhelpful thinking patterns and learning to see things from a balanced perspective,” Dobinson says.



It also means you have good and bad days; you can’t completely avoid negative or anxious thoughts. And realistic planning means you have something to look forward to. “Having goals and plans for the future increases our motivation, brings us happiness, and helps to focus our mind on important tasks. Planning things to look forward to, or setting a goal to overcome a past challenge, can be healthy ways to improve your general wellbeing,” Dobinson says. You have coping strategies It’s human to experience difficult emotions or setbacks, Dobinson says, but if you have a mental tool kit of coping strategies, it’s a sign of generally healthy mental wellbeing. Fostering a sense of resilience can help you cope with life’s difficulties.



Related Article Wellbeing It turns out this universal guilty pleasure is actually good for our health “This doesn’t mean you don’t experience negative emotions or stress, but that you’re able to navigate these stressors, ask for help, and adjust over time,” Dobinson says. Another indicator is being comfortable seeking support from a health professional when needed. So never be afraid to ask for help. World.title: Kyrgios tests positive to cocaine, faces lengthy ban from tennis
World.content:
Breaking SportTennisDrugs in sport Kyrgios tests positive to cocaine, faces lengthy ban from tennis Marc McGowan August 19, 2026 — 6:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Controversial Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios has taken full responsibility for making a “huge mistake” after testing positive for banned substance cocaine. The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) announced on Wednesday night (AEST) that it had provisionally suspended Kyrgios under the tennis anti-doping program. He has so far not appealed the decision. Nick Kyrgios is a former world No.13 who reached the 2022 men’s singles final at Wimbledon. Marijan Murat/Picture Alliance via Getty Images The 31-year-old provided a sample during an ATP 250 event in Mallorca, Spain, on June 22 before a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory confirmed the presence of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine, on July 17. Kyrgios’ provisional suspension started on August 4.



Related Article Wimbledon Kyrgios drama as he bids Wimbledon farewell; doubt surrounds Serena In a statement posted to his Instagram story on Wednesday, Kyrgios apologised for his actions and said he would take a break from social media and public life to “focus on getting myself right”. “I wanted you to hear this from me first. I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine,” Kyrgios posted. “I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it. I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets, and I’m deeply disappointed in myself. “I’m not going to make excuses, but I do want to give some context about where I’ve been. The last couple of years of injuries have taken a huge toll on me, both physically and mentally.



Nick Kyrgios’ apology on his official Instagram account. Instagram “My body hasn’t been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined. “I’ve always said I didn’t choose tennis – tennis chose me. But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I’ve ever had to face. At times I’ve felt helpless and alone. None of that excuses what I did. “However, the good news is that this has given me a wake-up call. For the next 28 days, I’ll be stepping away from social media and public life while I focus on getting myself right. “I’d ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly, the privacy of my family. I’m sorry. I’ll do the work and come back better.”



According to the ITIA, Kyrgios, the former world No.13 and 2022 Wimbledon finalist, is yet to appeal the provisional suspension. This masthead has contacted Kyrgios’ management. More to come

World.title: Governor-general ‘shocked and troubled’ by Swans sexual assault allegation
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAFL off-field behaviour Governor-general ‘shocked and troubled’ by Swans sexual assault allegation Natassia Chrysanthos August 19, 2026 — 6:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s Governor-General Sam Mostyn has said she is shocked and troubled by the alleged sexual assault investigation that has engulfed the Sydney Swans while warning that a lack of respect for women across the country remained a problem, particularly in sport. In a rare intervention from a head of state, Mostyn said that sports clubs and the community in general needed to be vigilant about women’s treatment while noting Australia still had “appalling statistics” when it came to domestic and sexual violence against women. Governor-General Sam Mostyn. Alex Ellinghausen Five Sydney Swans players were on Wednesday suspended for the rest of the season for breach of club behavioural standards as Victoria Police started investigating separate conduct of an allegation of sexual assault from Sunday night. A woman provided a written complaint to city police on Tuesday afternoon, although no charges have yet been laid. “I was shocked and troubled by the allegation of sexual assault … stemming from the weekend in Melbourne,” Ms Mostyn said, in comments first reported by the ABC on Wednesday evening.



“At times like this, we are reminded to never take for granted the need for constant vigilance for respectful treatment of women everywhere; across clubs, the AFL, sport, and the community generally. “The most important thing in moments like this is to fully accept responsibility, be accountable and take appropriate action.” Mostyn, a prominent businesswoman, became the first female member of the AFL commission in 2005 and joined the Swans board in 2017. She resigned from that position when Prime Minister Anthony Albanese appointed her as Australia’s 28th governor-general in 2024. She has commented on gender equality issues since taking the role, after a corporate career that often highlighted women’s issues. Last month, Mostyn publicly backed quotas to install more women in senior roles. However, she has typically refrained from discussing controversies or sensitive matters that are open to investigation, and it is extremely rare for a governor-general to comment on such issues. Mostyn said her thoughts were with the woman who made the sexual assault allegation, and that she hoped she was being supported.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Deeply sorry to everyone involved’: Suspended Swans speak out for first time “I am also devastated for the women of the Swans, whether they are players, staff, fans and everyone involved in the club and women across the industry who have been hurt by this incident,” she said. “Sadly, the lack of respect for women across the country remains an issue for us all to be concerned about, particularly in sport. We must all, men and women, constantly strive for respect for everyone, to educate our youngest players and fans, and that responsibility to educate is held by so many; administrators, leaders and players of the sport, all of whom shape culture. “I note Australia still has appalling statistics when it comes to domestic and sexual violence against women.” Mostyn said she believed great progress had been made to make sure women were represented in sport, particularly in women’s leagues.



“We have seen this magnificent and timely inclusion and celebration of women across our football codes, and today, little boys and girls know women are welcome and respected across our sporting landscape,” she said. But she said Australia needed to “remain committed to bringing more women into positions of influence in the AFL and all sports”, citing her own experience of joining the AFL commission as instructive in demonstrating why it was important to bring a woman’s perspective to the game. “We need more women inside the game, from coaching, administration, leadership and governance. And that’s also across all sport. The more diverse and representative people are in club culture and sports culture, the greater confidence we can have in safe places for women, and everyone,” she said. Mostyn said she had committed herself “to put care, kindness and respect at the centre of my work when I became governor-general”. Related Article Crime Isaac Heeney revealed as player at centre of sexual assault investigation



“I believe that is what most Australians want all our leaders and role models to show; that everyone can feel respected, welcome and safe in any workplace, sporting, or community context,” she said. “But again we must ensure that women are present and valued for their insights, experience and contribution to establishing respectful environments, at all levels of leadership, coaching, administration. Sport must be a safe place for everybody. Particularly women in the football codes. “We all have a duty to call out bad behaviour whenever we see it and always encourage and teach what respectful behaviour requires of us all.” Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek on Wednesday afternoon said she did not want to speak about individual cases, but said sporting codes should know how powerful their voices were. “I want to be very careful not to speak about any of the allegations or investigations underway in specific terms … I don’t want to prejudice any potential investigation,” she said on the ABC.



“I’d say a few things in general terms. Sporting codes, teams like the Swans have an incredibly important role in our community. They are the people who boys and young men look up to, they’re their heroes, they’re role models. And I am really pleased to hear some of the measures that the club’s taken today. “I think it is important to show that sporting clubs, schools, other institutions take allegations of sexual assault seriously. It is really important that in any discussion we centre victims and survivors of sexual assault. And hearing the club take strong measures is a really important step forward.” The Swans released a statement on behalf of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice on Wednesday evening. “We are deeply sorry to everyone involved. We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club,” the statement read. “We know we have let down our partners and families, members, supporters, teammates, the AFLW team, corporate partners and everyone at the club and the wider community. We accept the club sanction and apologise for the impact this has had on those involved. Our focus will now be on rebuilding trust with the club and the community.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis.
